(es) ladies and gentlemen, the commission would point out that the issues raised by the honourable member are linked in particular to respect for human dignity and the prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, principles which are common to all the member states of the union. these principles are laid down in article 6 of the treaty on european union and confirmed in articles 1 and 4 of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. the respect of these principles by states is guaranteed by the infringement procedure provided for in article 226 of the treaty on the european community and by the political procedure provided for in article 7 of the treaty on european union. according to the first, the commission may bring an action before the court of justice if the contested act falls within the scope of community law. the second provides that the commission or one third of the member states of the union may refer the matter to the council, meeting in the composition of heads of state or government, in the event of a serious and persistent breach of the principles referred to in article 6. the majority of cases dealt with by the questions raised by the honourable member concern asylum, immigration and the protection of the rights of third country nationals. these issues are within the scope of the community's powers. the commission has also begun to legislate on this subject in accordance with articles 61 and 63 of the ec treaty. the commission would point out, however, that the council of europe report to which the honourable member refers was followed by a detailed response from the greek authorities, which in the present situation provide a number of responses to the concerns expressed by the european committee for the prevention of torture. in any event, the commission will follow closely the development of the dialogue between the council of europe and the greek authorities.

in writing. - (el) the proposal on fundamental rights within the eu is, on the whole, positive. however, there are some paragraphs which are problematic, such as paragraph 78 on the ban on women entering mount athos. i believe that women's rights should not be assessed at this level but rather in areas such as employment, equal pay, domestic violence or the fight against human trafficking. i do not think that we can speak of freedom of movement in this small piece of land, which has its own sense of time and lives according to customs and traditions that are thousands of years old. soon we will be asking for freedom of establishment and enterprise, and we will see monasteries flooded with coca-cola stands. in a world where everything is being homogenized and plasticised, we must respect the cultural wealth inherited from the past, which does not influence modern society, and let mount athos continue its journey through time in peace. therefore, because of the presence of paragraph 78, i am obliged to reject the whole report.
in the case of greece, the resolution in mrs swiebel's report expresses a very negative view. on most of the points where criticism is directed at greece or where greece is urged to make improvements, either the relevant provisions of greek law have already been adjusted - and therefore the necessary improvements have been made - or the first steps towards such adjustment have been taken. the following examples are given as an indication: 1. we are urged (see paragraph 17) to abolish the death penalty. in doing so, it omits three things, namely that: (a) the death penalty has already been abolished, with the sole exception of the military penal code, and moreover only in respect of war crimes; (b) the draft law abolishing the death penalty in the military penal code is ready; (c) the death penalty, if imposed, is not carried out. the second. conscientious objection: (a) there is a new provision under which a person may be exempted from compulsory military service; the scheme is enshrined in the constitution; (b) under greek law this favourable treatment is no longer limited to persons who refuse to serve for religious reasons; the court of justice has also held that the principle of equal treatment for men and women in matters of religion and belief is not incompatible with the principle of equal treatment for men and women.
in writing. - (el) by voting in favour of the pirker report, a report rejected by the kke (communist party of greece), the european parliament laid the foundations for the materialisation of racist and xenophobic decisions aimed at making the eu immune to waves of immigration. the seville council decided to create a further hyper-nationalist and repressive mechanism, the european border guard corps, whose imminent establishment is in contradiction with the constitutions of the member states. for this reason, the commission decided to set up a hybrid counterpart to the border guards, which it calls the 'joint agency for the protection of the external borders'. it also decided to incorporate into community legislation another text of a clearly police nature, the 'common manual on the protection of external borders', after a previous revision which made it even more undemocratic. finally, the use of satellites and radars to monitor the eu's borders is even being considered, thanks to the galileo satellite navigation system. the register of surveillance and police services has been enriched by an additional service, scifa+, which will function as an orientation and coordination service. it is worrying to see that the report voted by the european parliament is more autocratic than the commission's statement. the european union is also committed to the development of a european security policy based on the principles of the rule of law, democracy and human rights. the report also contains criticisms of the adoption of propaganda concerning 'modified threat scenarios'; criticisms of the delay in the constitution of the border guard corps, etc.

mr president, it is indeed tragic that after 50 years of development aid, we find that not a single country has escaped from underdevelopment and poverty. many argue that globalization is the cause of the economic situation of the poorest countries. the truth is that the north's protectionist policy is contributing to the strangulation of key sectors of the south. the notion that poor countries can match the incomes of rich countries without international trade, without capital inflows and investments, is completely wrong. if poor countries rely on their own savings or wait to develop their own technology and skills, it will take them centuries. a society where a few become very rich and many very poor cannot really progress. hunger and extreme poverty are predominantly female, making racial inequality a major barrier to development. over the last decade, there has been an increase in women living in extreme poverty, which is linked to reproductive health problems, as the poorest women also have less access to health services and more unwanted children. almost half a million of all maternal deaths are in the developing world, and they die not because they choose to be mothers, but because they are poor. the chance of a woman dying from such causes is less than one in three thousand women in developed countries and as high as one in nineteen in africa. these numbers suggest that the benefits of globalization have not reached a large number of people. continuing poverty is holding this process back through open trade. the only solution is to defeat the two greatest enemies, on the one hand the resistance of many political leaders in the north who refuse to remove the barriers to the free movement of goods and people, and on the other the resistance of many political leaders in the south who refuse to give their citizens basic political, economic and human rights, which are a necessary condition for development.

mr president, the european union's intention to sacrifice small and mediumsized farmers and support for agriculture at european union level to the world trade organisation is obvious. the principle agricultural products on the pretext that it will increase international trade and benefit developing countries. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. international trade in agricultural products may have increased, wealth may have increased, but developing countries and their people have not only not benefited, but have been left worse off, with no room for growth, even for high-productivity countries like argentina. in contrast, multinational companies that produce and market agricultural products have increased their profits dramatically. the wto agreement will be similarly affected for three main reasons: the first relates to the pro-monopoly direction, such as gatt. the second concerns the international system of prices and subsidies for agricultural products, but also the international system of prices for industrial products. rich countries buy cheap agricultural products and sell expensive industrial products including medicines. the third reason is the relations of production and ownership of agricultural products in many developing countries, where agricultural land and agricultural products are owned by large multinationals, which produce them on a starvation wage. that is why the communist party of greece opposes the proposed agreement and does everything it can to coordinate the struggle of all the popular strata of all the countries for an international trade based on equality and mutual benefit.

the commission. greece's debt ratio is one of the highest in the community. it increased until the mid-1990s, peaking at over 110% of gdp in 1996. this was a consequence of growing budgetary imbalances and low growth in gross domestic product. stabilisation efforts with a view to participation in monetary union and improvements in key macroeconomic indicators have contributed to a reduction in the debt ratio, albeit at a very slow pace. the debt still represents 107% of gdp in 2001. three factors have influenced this development: the level of the primary balance, i.e. after financial payments, the growth rate of nominal gross domestic product and other autonomous or residual factors. these include financial operations which affect the volume of debt rather than the budget balance. in fact, the high level of adjustment of the debt ratio, which reached 7,1% of gdp in 2001 - and is still estimated at 4% of gdp in 2002 - meant that the evolution of the debt ratio did not fully reflect the evolution of the general government budgetary position, the achievement of rising high primary surpluses or the growth of gdp. moreover, the evolution of the public debt as described in the greek stability programme for 2002 has been partly affected by the revision of the statistical methods used in various financial transactions. this review was carried out in accordance with the system established by eurostat to meet the conditions set out in the esa 95, in our european system of national accounts. the statistical review carried out in 2002 resulted in an increase in the debt ratio in greece in 2001, which was 7 percentage points higher than the previously estimated figure. taking into account the new budgetary outlook resulting from this review, the updated stability programme envisages a reduction in the debt ratio equivalent to 1,7 percentage points in 2002, with an acceleration of this reduction from 2003 onwards, with a reduction of approximately 0,4 percentage points until the end of 2006. in fact, from 2003 onwards, the change in the debt ratio will correspond more closely to the level of the primary surplus. according to the commission's economic forecasts last autumn, greece's debt ratio is expected to decline until the end of 2004, albeit at a slower pace than the 2002 stability programme. for the period after 2004, when the updated stabilisation programme already allows for some decline in real output growth, a credible budgetary adjustment strategy will be necessary to ensure that the debt ratio envisaged in the programme is reduced. in this respect, the increased transparency of the public accounts achieved by the recent revision of the public accounts has increased the credibility of the public accounts and the budgetary adjustment strategy outlined in the greek stability programme.

- the agenda calls for the joint discussion of 9 questions by the council and the commission on the harmful effects of unexploded ordnance (antipersonnel mines and cluster bombs) and depleted uranium munitions.
mr president, i shall not go into the mines. the point is obvious. we have all seen images on television of children being mutilated, and more recently in many parts of the former yugoslavia. i shall devote the bulk of my speech to depleted uranium. natural uranium contains more than 99% of the isotope uranium 238 and very little uranium 235. uranium 235 is the one that is very good for fuel in nuclear reactors and is also used as a material in nuclear weapons. so it enriches the material to uranium 235 and what's left, the residue, which is mostly uranium 238, is the depleted uranium. this depleted uranium is used because it's very dense, it has a penetrating capacity, when used in bombs, they can go through floors, they can go through tank casings and so on. but it has the disadvantage that it evaporates in the explosion. and when it evaporates, most of it oxidizes. these oxides lead to soluble uranium salts that exist in a range of 10-15 kilometers and many times with the winds these can be carried several hundred kilometers, they can be inhaled, they can go into the water etc. the problem with uranium 238 is that while it has very weak a-radiation, meaning that i can hold it in my hand and not get any damage, if i inhale it, because there are phagocytes in the body that take these particles, they irradiate these cells very close to their genetic material, and that's where any dangerous energy of this depleted uranium is attributed. of course, the studies that have been carried out are not 100% proof of this action of uranium, but there are still many incidents which should make us very, very careful. that is exactly what parliament's resolution says, that because there are very likely to be public health risks and dangerous effects from exposure to depleted uranium, it would be good for the commission (that is point 7) to monitor exactly these investigations and everything related to depleted uranium and the possible widespread environmental pollution and the long-term risk to human health. it is quite logical that our parliament should be concerned with these kinds of matters, which it is good to take into account in order to avoid the use of these munitions because, i repeat, they have this great disadvantage. also, this depleted uranium has a lifespan of thousands of years. once some areas are infected, the contamination will remain for thousands of years. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's nuclear safety is not compromised by the use of chemical weapons. for all these reasons, i would like to ask my colleagues to vote in favour of this resolution, which i think, both on mines and on depleted uranium munitions, is exactly in line with the realities of today. i think that the european parliament should vote on it and the commission should also take up this matter and monitor it. i hope that the council and the greek presidency will do the same to help ottawa to ratify the convention, so that we do not have the use of landmines, but also for a moratorium, and possibly later for a complete cessation of the use of depleted uranium munitions.

commission. – mr president, perhaps i might deal with a few of the issues that were addressed, particularly in relation to health matters. this issue, as i indicated earlier, has been considered not just by the commission, and not just by the council of ministers, but also by parliament. as i mentioned earlier, the stoa report of may 2001 concluded, among other things, that in the light of the epidemiological studies on persons exposed to depleted uranium in iraq and the balkans, among a relatively small group of soldiers, who evidently had been exposed to depleted uranium during the gulf war, no health problems attributable to depleted uranium could be found. among the british gulf war veterans neither the overall death rate nor the occurrence of specific causes of death, such as cancer, are significantly different from those of a reference population. no association between the health problems of many gulf war veterans, that is gulf war syndrome, and suspected depleted uranium exposure could be found. in the case of german kfor soldiers in kosovo potentially exposed to depleted uranium, it could be demonstrated that no significant intake had occurred. preliminary results of a medical expertise show that the incidence of leukaemia among the italian kfor troops is not significantly higher than the incidence in a reference population. thus, it can be concluded that, so far, there is no scientific evidence of health damage among army personnel or civilian populations as a consequence of the use of du ammunition in the gulf war or the war in the balkans. controversial information and reports about the dramatic health effects of du among soldiers of the iraqi and yugoslav armies, and among the civilian population in the area concerned, do not withstand a peer review. the commission came to exactly the same view when it considered these issues and studies, as did the council. the stoa report went on to say that 'having comprehensively reviewed and cross-examined most of the specialised scientific literature, in particular the medical literature, judged reliable and trustworthy. having in mind the results provided by the medical observation over decades of workers in the uranium industry, as well as by the experiments with animals. taking into account the results of the recent investigations in iraq and in the balkans, of the effect on man and on the environment following the use of du', the use of du ammunition in iraq and the balkans 'neither has led to a serious widespread contamination of the environment nor represents an acute or appreciable long-term hazard for man's health'. it then it goes on to give a number of recommendations, none of which coincide with the views that have been expressed by the largely green members of parliament who have spoken here this evening. i should say that having regard to all of these scientific studies, the seriousness and comprehensiveness of the work that has been undertaken –including conscience. the same, i suspect, cannot be said of those who make allegations that are unfounded against people who are doing their best to provide proper answers to these questions.

commission. – madam president, this proposal for a council recommendation is based on article 152 of the treaty, which stipulates that community action complementing national measures is to cover the fight against the major health scourges. the treaty cites drugs and drugs-related harm in the following way: 'the community shall complement the member states' action in reducing drugs-related health damage, including information and prevention.' may i also remind you that one of its main initiatives in the fight against drugs - the eu drug strategy 2000-2004 - includes amongst its three main public health targets one to reduce substantially drugs-related health damage and the number of drugs-related deaths. the reported number of deaths related to drug overdose in the european union is approximately 7 000 per year. deaths indirectly related to drug use, such as aids, traffic accidents, violence or suicide, bring this figure to approximately 20 000 a year. preventing the use of illegal drugs is a top priority. this can be achieved by reducing both the supply and the demand for drugs. this proposed recommendation particularly covers the demand side and takes over where law enforcement fails to stop the supply of drugs. clearly, we should try to persuade people not to use illegal drugs in the first place. however, when an individual cannot be stopped from taking drugs, it is of vital importance that every effort is made to decrease the damage to the person involved, as well the indirect damage the user can cause to others. the addicted individual needs to be actively involved in these efforts. this is called risk reduction – or sometimes harm reduction or harm minimisation. this is what the main part of the recommendation is about. the risk reduction methods that feature in the recommendation are well established. they have been used in most or all of the member states, but to varying degrees. opiates, such as heroin, are the root cause of most drugs-related deaths. one of the oldest of the risk reduction methods is controlled use of methadone tablets as a substitute for injected heroin. methadone first appeared in the eu in the late 1960s in response to emerging opiate use. the emergence of hiv in the 1980s led to the introduction of needle- and syringe-exchange programmes. in recent years, the number of acute drugs-related deaths at eu level as a whole has stabilised, in spite of increasing drug use. many factors may have contributed to this development. injecting drugs has decreased in some countries and medical treatment of overdoses has improved. however, the risk reduction methods covered by this recommendation are likely to have made a large contribution to this favourable development. drug services need to be easily accessible, reaching out to the place where the drug user happens to be, not where we want him or her to be. these are termed 'outreach services'. such services should also be offered without unrealistic demands – sometimes called 'low threshold services'. the aim is to prevent further deterioration in the health and social circumstances of users and motivate them to seek treatment. the more controversial risk reduction methods are not mentioned in the present recommendation, although they are being used in some of the member states. methods such as heroin injections under supervision, injection rooms, open-drug scenes and on-the-spot anonymous testing of substances require more research and evaluation before they can be generally recommended. the recommendation emphasises evaluation as a key tool for improving drugs-related measures. the european monitoring centre for drugs and drug addiction in lisbon plays a crucial role in the development of key indicators for monitoring and comparing drug use in the member states. it also assists in providing guidelines for the evaluation of drugs-related projects and evaluates different programmes and policies. the commission has received invaluable help from the lisbon agency in preparing this recommendation, which i see as a positive step for drug users as well as public health in general.
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments. madam president, commissioner, unfortunately drug abuse is one of the most important social problems in the world, and this is a sign of the inadequacy of the measures and policies that have been put in place so far. the increase in drug use is also happening alongside other problems facing our societies today. the 2002 report of the european monitoring centre for drugs and drug addiction shows that the problem of drug use remains at relatively stable levels. in particular, it states that we have between 2 and 9 users per 1 000 inhabitants, aged 15 to 64, of whom between 500 000 and 1 000 000 are intravenous drug users, that is, heroin users. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens and mutagens is a good one, but it is not enough to say that the directive is a good one. i do not conceal from you that i would prefer the conditions to be met for this proposal to have a legislative content, because only through a common european policy or even a legislative approach will our policies be effective. however, i believe that the recommendations proposed are a very important step towards protecting the public health but also the individual health of users and we are also sending the right political message that addicts are patients in need of health and social care, and not just offenders as most societies believe today. the amendments we tabled are mainly concerned with a more detailed list of the specific actions that each local community must take in order to obtain the maximum possible results in this difficult and sensitive area. the awareness of citizens towards acceptance of treatment programmes of different approaches and other user protection measures is a necessary prerequisite for the implementation of the proposed recommendations. in particular, when we talk about harm reduction measures, the main objective is still the recovery of the user. but we know that a significant number of addicts are not in treatment and that this group is the one that has the most problems. the health education of this group is the basis for limiting the spread of dangerous infectious diseases such as hepatitis, aids, tuberculosis. it also leads users to safer use of technology and ultimately to a healthier lifestyle. it is also of the utmost importance to include measures intended for high-risk environments such as prisons. according to european union reports, the proportion of prisoners using drugs in prison varies between 29% and 86% in different prisons and countries. prisoners are extremely exposed to disease through the sharing of needles and syringes, as well as through sexual contact. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union's prisoners are not subject to the same treatment as other prisoners. the commission is aware that the debate on drugs has been going on for several years now and that there are many and often conflicting views. however, we have succeeded, and i thank all my colleagues, and especially the shadow rapporteurs, for their cooperation, in bringing to the house today a relatively unanimous proposal despite the initial 103 amendments. i believe that if the member states implement even part of the proposed measures, both users and their families and european citizens will feel that we really want to do something about this complex and difficult problem.

commission. – the commission closely follows the human rights situation in zimbabwe. it is aware that the conditions remain volatile and is deeply concerned regarding the increased incidence of politically motivated violence observed recently. in view of the gravity of the situation, the commission proposed to the council the extension of the measures against zimbabwe under article 96 of the cotonou agreement, which were adopted in february last year. these measures redirect funds to social sectors and to areas which benefit directly the population. this is for a renewable period of one year. the commission agrees with the presidency's proposal for a new common position amending and extending sanctions, such as the visa ban and freeze of assets against zimbabwe, for the same additional period of one year. the commission is informed that approximately eur 770 000 have been frozen in accounts in member states or their dependent territories in accordance with the council's position. community assistance continues to contribute to projects which directly support the population in the field of democratisation, respect for human rights and the rule of law; the european initiative for democracy and human rights includes zimbabwe as a focal country. the commission is particularly concerned about the food crisis in zimbabwe and has been very actively involved in responding to the situation. between april and december 2002, we committed about eur 80 million in emergency aid and humanitarian aid. the commission believes that all avenues for dialogue should be explored to improve the situation in zimbabwe. we will support any peer pressure that the international community, and the heads of state in africa in particular, may put on the zimbabwean government in the area of respect for the essential elements of the cotonou agreement: human rights, democracy and the rule of law. (applause)

the commission is aware of the fact that the european parliament has been asked to make a statement on the subject of the directive on the transport of dangerous goods. we often lament that europe could also use maritime transport as an alternative to road transport, to land transport in general. however, we now find that sometimes the very people who say we have to promote shipping more put up obstacles in order to achieve a more competitive and more adapted shipping system. we clearly need to improve the efficiency of port services, and that is what this initiative is about. we need to improve the efficiency of these services, to put an end to monopoly situations which sometimes mean that the same services cost three or four times more in one port than in another in the european union, which indicates that something is wrong, and - i repeat - all this by ensuring, excluding or setting limits and guarantees so that the aspects relating to maritime safety are kept at the highest level. we in the commission believe that the council's common position takes account to a large extent of the amendments adopted by parliament at first reading and that it is a balanced solution to achieve these objectives and i think it would be a real mistake not to maintain this balance, to change the broad lines of balance that have been established in the council. in this connection, ladies and gentlemen, i shall explain the commission's position on the proposed amendments. some of them clearly improve the council's common position and therefore the commission accepts them in whole, in principle or in part. that is to say, once again, the commission is making an effort to make the codecision system work as well as possible. i would first like to refer to the amendments which make the provisions of the commission directive on transparency relevant to ports to which the directive applies. this is the objective which we all shared from the beginning and i regret that the rapporteur, mr jarzembowski, considers that what has been said there is insufficient. i shall, however, refer in particular to some of the amendments dealing with these aspects. secondly, we can accept amendment no 11 - which refers to a lower frequency of revision of the list of ports of a very seasonal nature - and amendments nos 5 and 27 - which provide examples of expensive movable property which could therefore be equated with immovable property when considering depreciation or residual costs. we can also support all those amendments which, without going into detail, we believe constitute appropriate contributions to the common position or which provide additional clarification, in one way or another, to the final text. i would like to congratulate mr jarzembowski and the committee on transport in general once again on the work they have done. however, some amendments seem to seek to slow down, even paralyse, the efforts to promote this dynamism of european ports, to improve, as i said before, the potential of long-distance maritime transport, facilitating our exports in the world, but also short-distance, thus providing an alternative to land transport. it is therefore clear that we cannot support amendments nos 36 and 66 which call for the council's common position to be rejected. that said, i would like to make a few brief references to other matters which mr jarzembowski has spoken about. firstly, the question of competition between ports. i know that this is a matter of great concern to the rapporteur and other members, and i also understand that we must make progress on this. that is why i have proposed accepting the amendments which propose the inclusion of ports in the commission's directive on transparency. the commission understands the concern. in fact, our recent document on this subject is proof of our willingness to solve the problem while respecting the provisions of the treaty, mr jarzembowski, that is to say, state aid has a framework - which is what we have raised - but it cannot simply be regulated, it is the treaty itself which imposes the regulatory framework. we must clarify this to avoid, as i said, any doubts or legal uncertainties. and that is why, mr jarzembowski, i say that amendment no 15 goes beyond such provisions and we cannot accept it. we are, however, prepared to try to find a solution acceptable to all with the honourable members. in this sense, amendment no 10, duly amended, with some important adjustments in line with the solution we can find, could give us a basis for finding that compromise formula. i would ask that we work as hard as we can to find her as soon as possible. as regards amendment no 16, i would remind you that the commission itself, in the context of the so-called 'package of port measures', has already carried out a study such as the one you are asking for and the cooperation from ports was unfortunately limited. secondly, mr jarzembowski has spoken of the practice of self-help. in every modern port this practice should be allowed where possible, both for on-board and shore-based operations. the common position reflects this desire to send a message of progress and not of backwardness and rigidity. a message of progress, of progress, but with all the guarantees. in this connection, it is clearly stated that such actions must comply with the social, environmental and safety standards required in each port and that this requirement is essential in order to be able to carry out such self-help. the amendments which seriously restrict this approach - because they restrict self-help operations in various ways - by limiting them exclusively to seafarers, cannot be accepted. the commission's proposal is that the european union should be able to take part in the negotiations on the future of the european union, and that the european union should be able to take part in the negotiations on the future of the european union. because the additional limitation on vessels flying the union flag would put the community at odds with its partners in the world and that too must be avoided. finally, we have always considered that the practice is a commercial service. access to such a service should therefore be regulated by the treaty and by this directive. for this reason, we support the consensus reached in the common position that authorizations should be subject to particularly strict criteria relating to public service obligations and maritime safety - and again we return to the reality of each port. but this approach can be adapted by means of port-specific solutions, which allow self-help in the field of practice in the form of exemption certificates under certain conditions. in conclusion, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, tomorrow's vote will have a major impact on the legislative process. the commission has always been ready to find constructive solutions with the european parliament. i would remind you once again that our overall objective is to ensure that the booming port services industry is ready to meet the challenges ahead. moreover, the future european transport system will only be successful with efficient and far-sighted ports. so once again i would ask for your support for this commission proposal and congratulate the rapporteur, mr jarzembowski, and the whole team who have worked on this text, and the honourable members for their attention.

(el) in the name of creating a common framework and providing better port services, the private sector has been made to pay for taking over tasks that until now have been part of the public service. the existing ports will be given the opportunity to offer more services in any sector they consider profitable. the public administration and the provider of the essential service, in turn, take care of the necessary though unprofitable actions. under the new system, the terms and conditions and the authorisations are decided by a decision-making centre which is not the same as the previous provider of port services, since the same body cannot be both the service provider and the port authority. companies providing port services shall comply with transparency requirements in their dealings with public authorities. the private sector does not appear to be subject to a similar requirement. the directive makes special reference to workers. article 6 (5) of the directive provides that a service provider is entitled to recruit staff of his choice, but it does not provide for qualifications or training. we want port services that are transparent and provide a level playing field for all, that protect workers' rights, the environment and port safety.

in writing. - (el) the division of the market between the monopolies and the powerful of this world, in the framework of the wto, is not limited to industrial and agricultural products, but also extends to services. we are witnessing, in a climate of opacity, an intensification of discussions on the conditions for the penetration of foreign capital in the fields of transport, telecommunications, energy, banking, water distribution, health, education and culture, according to the principle "everything is bought and everything is sold", with the least developed countries in mind, as the multinationals are ready to bleed even more. the essential precondition is the privatisation and liberalisation of all areas still in the hands of the public sector. the greek communist party is opposed to this process. we condemn the greed of monopolies, the plundering of national wealth, the ruthless exploitation of workers, the appalling working conditions, the attack on social benefits. we also condemn the hypocrisy of all those who claim that trade liberalization, the opening up of markets, the removal of all obstacles to the immunity of big capital will lead to development. we are defending, both for greece and for all the countries of the world, public ownership and management of the basic sectors of the economy, we are fighting for a high-quality public health and education system, for the unhindered development of culture, based on respect for the peculiarities of each people.

in writing. - (el) there is an attempt to solve the problem of unemployment by intensifying liberal monetary policies and continuing with financial austerity, while forgetting that these same policies are responsible for the current crisis and the high unemployment rate. under the misleading title adopted in lisbon 'for sustainable development and full employment', and despite the increase in inequalities, member states are called upon to implement structural reforms leading to the distribution of unemployment, the generalization of flexible forms of work, uncertainty, insecurity for employees and the reduction of the cost of wages in order to ensure that large companies have a steady increase in their earnings. the widespread longterm unemployment, which has been affecting workers for several decades and now exceeds 10%, is now accompanied by a widespread use of temporary and provisional forms of work. under the guise of demographic change and the viability of funds, the extension of working time is proposed according to the logic of "active ageing" and the upheaval of the insurance and pension system. increasing investment will not solve the problem, since most of it is in technological equipment, which reduces jobs instead of increasing them. we oppose eu policies, based on the stability pact and the lisbon process, because they do not meet the needs of workers, farmers and small and medium-sized enterprises; because they aim to reduce workers' rights and they obey the laws of big business.

- the agenda calls for the commission's statement on the transfer of personal data by airlines to the us immigration service.
commission. – mr president, if you agree, as indicated on the board, this commissioner – who is less knowledgeable than his colleague – could begin the debate and then my colleague commissioner bolkestein will continue, as this issue touches on both our competences. i repeat what i said at the outset of the previous debate, and offer my apologies to parliament that i will have to leave early, though my distinguished colleague will be here until the end of the debate. i explained in the last debate that i am due to fly to croatia and belgrade later this afternoon and, not least because of the tragic events today, i know that parliament will understand that. let me now turn to the business in hand. the aviation and security act, passed by the us congress on 19 november 2001, is one of a series of laws introduced in the united states after 11 september 2001, with one overriding aim: to enhance national security, in particular through transport security measures. the basic aim is to prevent terrorist acts by detecting potential perpetrators before they enter the country. in this context, the united states congress has required that carriers make passenger name record information available to us customs upon request. the commission shares the security concerns of the united states. nevertheless, the united states measures have raised concern with regard to the respect of community and member states’ laws on data protection. airlines operating flights across the atlantic risked being caught between two sets of incompatible measures and suffering severe losses as a result of penalties the united states threatened to impose, including fines and even the withdrawal of landing rights. passengers - between 10 and 11 million a year - would have also suffered from the disrupted air traffic and from the time-consuming 'secondary' checks that the united states planned to introduce at point of entry. moreover, airlines not in compliance risked being seen as higher security risks, with potential consequences for significant falls in passenger numbers. the stakes, therefore, were very high and the consequences of not acting would have been extremely serious. we had to ensure, as far as we could, that the important interests of european union citizens in preserving their right to privacy was balanced against the need to protect many thousands of jobs in our airlines and associated industries like travel agencies. i want to assure this house that, right from the outset, the european commission has done its utmost to try to engage the united states in a discussion on how to find a solution compatible with both sets of legislation and one that would ensure legal certainty for all concerned. the european commission has assumed its responsibilities and in recent weeks undertook difficult discussions to overcome a stalemate created by the united states initially taking our concerns lightly and not responding to our questions. in fact, the european commission had raised this issue with the united states on numerous occasions, with particular emphasis since the us customs service issued its interim rule of 19 june 2002, containing the concrete implementation methods. as a result of these efforts by the commission, the united states first postponed the entry into force of the new requirements until 5 february and then agreed to waive the imposition of penalties on non-complying airlines until 5 march. following a high-level meeting on 17 and 18 february on access to personal data contained in passenger name records, both sides issued a joint statement which sets out the steps that need to be taken to reach a mutually satisfactory and legally certain solution to this issue. further talks took place on 4 march, as a result of which the united states has given additional undertakings with respect to the handling and protection of sensitive data. i am also aware that questions have been raised as to the legal basis for the action undertaken so far by the commission. this, as my colleague commissioner bolkestein will explain in more detail, seems to be founded on a misunderstanding. there has been no 'agreement' and no 'decision' so far. instead, we have engaged with the united states authorities in an intensive dialogue aimed at obtaining the necessary guarantees regarding the proper handling and use of the data concerned by the us side. both sides are now committed to continuing their discussions in order to find a more legally secure solution. the possibility of such discussions is provided for in the data protection directive, as the initial and necessary steps towards the adequacy finding provided for in its article 25(6). following comitology procedures, the draft commission decision will then have to be discussed by this house before being finalised. in the interim, we have obtained from the united states a provisional set of undertakings on how they will protect the personal data they access and a specific commitment not to make use of any sensitive data for profiling purposes. before passing the debate to my distinguished colleague to provide honourable members with further details on this issue, i would like to ask this house to recognise the considerable efforts made by the commission and the positive results we have achieved so far – even if these still have to be finalised – and i hope parliament will join forces with us in obtaining from the united states the necessary data protection guarantees for european citizens so that a permanent solution to the problem can be achieved. i should like to make one final personal remark. the whole house recognises how the events of 11 september produced a real feeling of vulnerability and shock in the united states. the house will recognise the concern in the united states to put in place measures to ensure that further terrorist attacks are less, rather than more, likely in the future. like a number of honourable members, i come from a country which has also had to take steps to deal with terrorist threats. that said, i hope that we can engage the united states at a much earlier stage in the policy-making process in discussing these security issues. if we can have a dialogue earlier in the process, it will be easier to avoid the sort of political difficulties that we have had from time to time over the last year. there should be no difference between us at all on the importance of putting in place security measures which are recognised as being reasonable by both sides. it would be easier to do that if we could talk more openly and earlier about these sorts of measures.

the commission's new strategy for consumer protection is ambitious, mr president. it represents the quality of life of the consumer: protection against unjustified practices, reduction of unjustified price differences between countries, the possibility of approaching a market of 350 million people with confidence, and the guarantee of the credibility of consumer organizations themselves. we must congratulate the commission on the rich research work and, of course, the rapporteurs on their improved proposals. but the road isn't paved with flowers. the obstacles and technical difficulties are many. first of all, businessmen and a number of colleagues must be convinced that the establishment of a regulatory framework is not contrary to the logic of competition but is one of the basic conditions for effective competition. secondly, everyone must be convinced that comprehensive consumer protection is not achieved by counting only business-consumer relations but also horizontal relations between businesses, since the common objective is to make the market work more efficiently and to protect consumers more effectively. the green paper, for example, should also consider the proposal for a regulation on sales promotion alongside its own proposals. as regards the method of dealing with this, it is right to give priority to a coherent framework directive which would incorporate certain basic principles, such as the prohibition of conduct which offends morals, the principle of good faith, the principle of fair trading practices. this method reduces the need for detailed regulation and allows for a rapid response to the proliferation of unfair inventions and unlawful practices. moreover, even the legal systems of central europe, which are familiar with the detailed regulations, increasingly rely on the general clauses to adapt the law to changing situations. this method proved valuable and made it possible to modernize the law. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. the flexible approach to the framework directive is also compatible with the policy of promoting self-regulation, which should be given priority, but on two conditions: firstly, there should be a general time-frame within which the parties concerned are invited to agree and, secondly, there should be a common framework defining the responsibilities arising from compliance with the obligations laid down in self-regulation. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial instruments are not used to the detriment of the community's own resources. the choice is difficult because on the one hand we want to ensure that harmonization does not lead to a reduction in the level of protection, and on the other hand maximalist proposals usually hinder the harmonization process. i think we should proceed on the basis of maximum harmonization and, where appropriate, selectively, towards minimum harmonization. in conclusion, mr president, i should like to say a few words about the special attention to be paid to consumer organizations. the question of representativeness and transparency should concern us because consumer organizations today are themselves a problem for consumer protection.
in writing. - (el) for the european union, the causes of unemployment and poverty of women are not due to capitalist exploitation. the causes are the lower level of qualifications of women, the burden of family responsibilities, reactionary views that encourage discrimination between the sexes. instead of providing stable full-time employment, part-time work is encouraged and anti-pedagogical rapid training courses are encouraged, transforming women into a flexible and cheap labour force. not only does the 3rd csf not allow women to take care of themselves, but it subsidizes employers so that they can weaken workers' rights, with most of the subsidies going to infrastructure work, which favors large companies. in the name of equality, the inclusion of the gender dimension in the various policies has reversed, within the strict anti-people economic policy, the provisions in favour of women, which worsen the situation of women. in addition, proposals are made for further reductions in the family allowance system and for private sector participation in health, education and social security projects and infrastructure. we are in favour of regulations for women's work provided they are provided free of charge. we oppose the promotion of flexible working hours in the name of reconciling work and family obligations. we are in favour of stable full-time work, the strengthening and extension of social and labour rights. the agenda calls for the report (a5-0077/2003) by mr brok and mr wynn, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy, and the committee on budgets, containing the european parliament's recommendations to the council on the introduction of a financial framework in the draft accession treaty. i should like to inform the house that the greek presidency has already informed the european parliament some time ago that the president-in-office of the council should arrive at the airport immediately after his speech in order to be in greece this evening and to be able to attend the meeting tomorrow between the council and the representatives of the latin american countries. the president is confident that the house will understand.
commission. – mr president, i am very pleased to be able to join the house on this debate on the report on the staff regulations, not only because it is always an honour to speak in this house but also because when there has been a very extended period of consideration and so many meetings, a certain family feeling develops. i am very pleased, therefore, to join so many friends tonight who have been my partners in discussion for what seems like an extremely long time. it was, however, a very worthwhile experience. i should like to start by expressing my very deep gratitude to the rapporteurs, mr harbour and mr medina ortega for their very thorough, thoughtful and constructive work on this important issue of the reform of the staff regulations. i also pay tribute to the intensive efforts undertaken by the other members of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market and to the opinion-giving committees and their draftspersons. very substantial work has been done in this house by everyone concerned. i know that the staff of the institutions will recognise the fact that serious and committed attention has been given by parliament to their statute, their employment conditions and their future. i think it will assist the house if i begin by referring to the issues raised in the oral question tabled by four political groups in the house. i was naturally going to highlight several pension issues in my statement this evening. i therefore welcome the questions because they give me the first opportunity since last wednesday's general affairs council to focus explicitly and publicly on those matters. responding to the question may mean that i take a little more time than was originally anticipated. i hope that in a good cause you will bear with me. to help to ensure clarity i should like to ask the house to refer to the draft guidelines that were adopted without change as the conclusions of the general affairs council of 18-19 march 2003. that document has been circulated. i regret that it is only in french and english at this juncture. if honourable members look at paragraph b of those conclusions they will see that the council instructed coreper to prepare a more detailed position, ‘on the issue of adaptation of the pension system’. if members then turn to paragraph d, they will see that the council called on the commission to ‘table by april 2003 a detailed, technical working document setting out a proposal to guarantee actuarial balance as from 1 january 2004’. examination of those paragraphs will show that the only request to the commission was for a proposal for the methodology for a study which would then facilitate calculation of the contributions required to ensure actuarial balance in the pension system. therefore there was no request to the commission to submit, in the words of the question, a detailed document that includes a change in the pension scheme. obviously, the commission will not be producing such a document at any stage. we have never produced such a document and we are not going to do it now. achieving and maintaining an actuarial balance is clearly a somewhat different issue. as honourable members will know, this has always been the obligation under the present article 83(4) of the staff regulations, even though the requirement has not been made consistently operational. the commission's proposal on modernisation of the staff regulations has always, therefore, included a commitment to ensure actuarial balance. of course, the issue was discussed and negotiated in detail with the trade unions and in the interinstitutional staff regulations committee well before the commission proposal went to the council and came to this house last year. so, there is nothing new about the commission's commitment to secure actuarial balance. there is nothing that has not been fully debated and assessed. there is nothing that was not made known and made clear to parliament and the members of the eu civil service and their staff representatives. all that the reference in the general affairs council conclusions relates to is the need for an up-to-date actuarial study that will enable the council and the eu civil service to know, well before 1 january 2004, exactly what the contribution rates by member states and by staff will be. meanwhile, the instruction to coreper in the general affairs council conclusions is to provide a more detailed position on adaptation of the pension system that, in the words of the conclusions, is more consistent with the trends prevailing in member states. that in itself is not surprising since it is obvious that demographic changes, the lisbon strategy and indeed the policy approach of the commission and of this house to so-called 'active ageing' will always ensure that member state governments give attention to issues of retirement and pensions. that reality has in fact ensured that several member state delegations have put forward a paper on pension parameters for the european union civil service, and it is being considered by the council. our response has been to point out that whilst we recognise the need to ensure consistency with the social and economic policy on employment and ageing which we, in the commission, advocate, we also emphatically require proper account to be taken of some basic facts about the employment age profile of the european union civil service, which are of great relevance to any consideration of pension parameters. those facts are, in brief: first that that average starting age of employment in the eu civil service is 32 years and 34 years for policy grade officials. any calculations that made a full pension dependant on more than 35 years of employment and payments would consequently be entirely unrealistic. second, there is the fact that, as your rapporteurs point out, whilst the official pensionable age in the eu civil service is relatively low at 60 years, the average real retirement age of 63.1 years is about three years later than the average retirement age in member states and one year later than in the member state with the highest average retirement age. in many respects therefore, we are implementing a core policy of the lisbon strategy and we have been doing so for several decades. against that background and in the context of actuarial balance, the commission has, in the course of negotiations, indicated some willingness to consider a degree of possible modification of the formal pensionable age. i should like to emphasise that there has been absolutely no conclusion of any kind on that point, or indeed on the other points. in this and in all other matters we have strongly emphasised the need to ensure that the acquired rights and legitimate expectations of present staff are properly respected. that clearly manifests our position. it answers the first question in the oral question. for reasons of emphasis i repeat that any discussion of any potential changes would have to fulfil that requirement on acquired rights and legitimate expectations. increased understanding of those facts induced the council to ask coreper to go away and, as the conclusions of the council show, prepare a more detailed position by the april general affairs council. in addition and to complete the picture, the gac conclusions include paragraph c that proposes further discussions on the weightings that are currently applied to eu civil service pensions in different member states. i know that there are a number of amendments before the house relating to these weightings. the issue is a source of general concern in this house and indeed in the council.since we are in negotiations, the commission can only say at this juncture that we hear those concerns and while we may not support the amendments that have so far been offered, we are aware of the need to deal with this matter within the overall balance of the negotiated final package. i reiterate that in this context, as well as in the wider spheres of reform, the commission will at all times actively seek to uphold the accumulated rights and legitimate expectations of current staff. that is a principle that we uphold and it is one that is understood by member states. i also emphasise that we are conducting the negotiations on the basis of the fundamental principle that nothing is agreed until everything is agreed. any decision on any issue would be subject to reaching an agreement that is mutually satisfactory in overall terms. i would add that we are engaged in complex and sometimes necessarily delicate negotiations; we are not engaged in polemical exchanges. we have confidence in the strength and the realism of our arguments and of our arithmetic. we will continue to strive to ensure that our partners in negotiation in the council will accept both the arguments and the arithmetic. that, obviously, is our sustained and unchanging objective. i regret that i have had to take time to give a detailed response on the important question put by honourable members. i think you will understand that i wanted to give full answers to the questions on this important issue of pensions. i warmly welcome the fact that the report from the committee on legal affairs and the internal market before this house for debate reiterates strong support, as we have heard from the rapporteurs, for the overall reform package and does so in serious, practical terms. in particular i welcome the realistic commitment to the importance of maintaining competitive levels of pay and pensions; a commitment to the introduction of what has become known in shorthand as a promotion guarantee on a collective basis – and i emphasise a collective basis; and a commitment to the inclusion in the staff regulations of 'the method' as the rational, economical and stable means for adjusting pay and pensions. moreover, i am pleased to say that the guidelines adopted by the general affairs council of 18-19 march 2003 echo many of the principles stated by messrs harbour and medina ortega in their explanatory statement and they are equally reflected in numerous amendments before us today. in particular, the guidelines in the council conclusions – paragraphs e, f and g respectively – express support for the broad pay and allowances proposals as a good basis, support the transitional arrangements for the new career system and express an openness towards the inclusion, on a finite basis, of the 'the method' in the staff regulations. in response to the amendments, i will first list the many that the commission can readily support. indeed, i will summarise them because i do not want to test the patience of the house. amendments nos 7, 8, 9 and 48 on the strengthening of interinstitutional cooperation; amendment no 20 on whistleblowing, amendments nos 12 and 14; amendment no 13 on the opening of the assistant 1 to assistant 3 career bracket for specific duties including the duties of parliamentary ushers; amendments nos 9, 25, 48, 50 and 51 tabled by the rapporteurs relating to the status of the staff of the political groups – this means of course that the commission cannot support amendments nos 32 and 60 which go well beyond the position set out wisely by the rapporteurs; amendment no 17 on sexual harassment, we can accept; amendment no 18, amendment no 19, amendments nos 33, 34 and 35 on staff absences; amendments nos 42, 43 and 44 on disciplinary procedures; amendment no 38 on the duration of the membership of the joint advisory committee for professional incompetence – that does not mean that it is in favour of incompetence, of course – it should be the joint advisory committee on professional incompetence. there is second group of amendments on which the commission is prepared to maintain an open mind during negotiations on the overall package or to accept some of the amendments, at least in part. the commission cannot at this juncture give a positive response to amendments on weighted pensions. however, as i said, we are of course conscious of the widespread political concerns relating to pension coefficients and of the need to deal with the matter within the overall balance of the total package. the commission is prepared to accept amendments nos 52 and 54 on the limitation of levels of function of contract agents and on the duration of those contracts; amendments nos 14, 15, 26, 29 and 30 relate to central provisions in the context of a new career system, article 5(3) on the criteria for appointments to the administrator and assistant function groups; article 31 on the organisation of competitions for higher grades, including middle management grades, and article 45 on the certification procedure for transfers from assistant to administrative function groups. all of these articles have, i am glad to say, been subject to intense discussions in council and coreper. the compromises reached as recently as last week will be seen to reflect many, if not all, of the objectives aimed at by members of this house in their amendments. article 31 now allows for the organisation of competitions, for instance, at administrator grades 9, 10, 11 or, on an exceptional basis, 12. remembering that administrator grade 12 will correspond to a higher level than today's grade a4, the total number of candidates appointed to vacant posts at these grades will not exceed 20% of the total number of the appointments by external recruitment to the administrator function group in any one year. that compromise goes further than the outcome sought, for example, by amendment no 26. on the certification procedure, article 45a now makes provision, in paragraph 2, for the european personnel selection office to determine the contents of all examinations organised by the institutions in order to ensure that the basic requirements of a transfer are met in a harmonised and consistent manner. that should make amendment no 30 redundant. on amendments nos 58 and 59 on members' assistants, this house knows the commission has been and always will be very aware and sympathetic to the concerns about this issue in parliament. honourable members will however be aware that of course several member states do not share our joint enthusiasm and there is much work to be done independently of the negotiations on the staff statute. on amendments nos 71 to 74 inclusive, on the recruitment of third country nationals with a permanent right of residence, the commission is aware that there is a discussion amongst political groups about the possibility of finding a compromise arrangement on this issue which is of concern to many honourable members. while sympathetic, the commission is not in a position to accept these amendments as they are currently formulated and therefore i have to reserve my position on this question for the time being. finally, and i am grateful for the patience of the house, there are inevitably some amendments which the commission cannot accept because they would tend to detract from the overall proposal. i will just pick a few, by no means an exhaustive list, but i must say it is outweighed by the number of amendments that we are readily accepting. we cannot accept amendment no 16, amendments nos 14, 15, 26, 29, 30 and 75 – for the reason that i mentioned earlier, i.e. that they are unnecessary because of positive developments in council on these questions; amendments nos 53, 55 and 76 on contract agents – because, as i said earlier, the commission supports amendments nos 52 and 54 from the committee on legal affairs and the internal market; amendment no 32 on the extension of article 50 to administrator grade 12 – we do not think that would be appropriate; amendment no 63 on sexual harassment where the commission supports the text put by the rapporteurs in amendment no 17, and finally amendment no 64 on the expatriation allowance, for the very direct reason that the commission retains the view that the allowance for staff who are expatriate workers is objectively justified and indeed objectively necessary. as the house knows, we have from the outset been committed to providing reforms in the staff regulations which would facilitate radical modernisation whilst upholding the current conditions of employment and improving the career development of members of the european union civil service. the reasons for that are, i hope, recognised to be practical and justified and not insular or conservative. there is a direct connection between reform, motivation and necessary material security. it is both realistic and relevant to acknowledge and to provide for that. this very substantial report from honourable members recognises that practical reality and is a significant step towards the fulfilment of our commitments. i warmly thank all who have been engaged in the compilation of parliament's view and i very much look forward to the adoption of the report in the house tomorrow morning.
the european commission, mr president, despite all the claims to the contrary, is a political reality and has a growing public sphere in which its rapidly expanding separate administration is central. but while this administration is constantly being enlarged and given new tasks, the necessary adjustments have not yet been made. the amendment of the staff regulations of its staff is more necessary than ever to achieve the modernisation of the personnel policy. we all know that technological progress has upended the data on staff organization, something the private sector has long recognised. we also know that the european union is promoting a number of policies, such as improving the quality of work and measures to combat discrimination, the adaptation of working life to family life and flexibility in employment. it would be strange if all these policies which it promotes for european society and european enterprises were not integrated into its own bureaucratic apparatus and if it did not set itself the example of a new model of public administration. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect, and i am sure that the commission will be able to support them. the first concerns the adoption of an amendment introducing a common rate for calculating pensions, irrespective of the place of residence of pensioners. the commission's proposal to introduce correction coefficients to adjust the amount of the pension to the purchasing power of the place of residence of pensioners is contrary to the community principle of equality and to the right of free movement. i support the amendment by our group on the need to ensure a climate of peace within the administrative departments of the institutions. it is important to stress that in the new world of work that is coming our way, ensuring mutual trust between all the players is a key element in increasing productivity. finally, i think we should accept our group's amendment which proposes that fixed-term contracts be converted into indefinite contracts where a five-year contract has been renewed for another five years. we think that this, combined with the hiring of contractors, achieves flexibility with the necessary protection.
the committee on constitutional affairs has adopted a number of amendments to the treaty on european union, including the amendment to article 3 of the treaty on european union, which provides for the adoption of a new constitution. mr president, i should first like to congratulate mrs theato on the excellent work she has presented. the committee on constitutional affairs has voted in favour of the creation of the european public prosecutor's office. and he said yes because he believes that the problems facing the european union at the moment need a more systematic approach and a more systematic approach. the commission has also taken the view that the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a good one. the first concerns the powers of the european prosecutor. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. it is a sad reality, unfortunately, but it is a reality. but he pointed out that the intergovernmental relations and the collective structures towards which the member states are moving require that the door of the powers of the european prosecutor be left open so that in the future, if necessary, other powers may be added to deal with other crimes, and you know very well that, unfortunately, the current international system generates new crimes. the second point that the committee on constitutional affairs points out is the role of the european parliament in relation to the institution of the european public prosecutor. we believe that the european parliament, which first highlighted the issues and problems with pan-european crime, should be the institution to which the european prosecutor will be accountable.
