commission. – mr president, i am pleased to have this opportunity to inform this house of the circumstances surrounding the condition known as severe acute respiratory syndrome, or sars, to use the acronym. it can be divided into a number of different questions. what is it? where does it come from? how does it spread? how can we stop it? this syndrome is a respiratory disease that has recently been reported in asia, north america and europe. the illness usually begins with a fever, sometimes associated with other symptoms such as chills, headache and body aches. after two to ten days sars patients may develop a cough that might progress to difficulties in breathing. in 10 to 20% of cases patients will require mechanical ventilation. it is estimated that in 4% of cases sars proves to be fatal. at present no treatment beyond good intensive and supportive care has been consistently shown to improve the condition of persons with sars. in relation to the causative agent, the scientists have detected a previously unrecognised virus belonging to the family of coronaviruses in patients with sars. while the new coronavirus is still the leading hypothesis for the cause of sars, other viruses are still under investigation as potential causes. on the question of transmission, the principal way sars appears to be spread is through respiratory secretions called droplets, namely, when someone with sars coughs or sneezes droplets into the air and someone else breathes them in. nevertheless, other ways of transmission cannot be ruled out, such as direct close contact with an infected person. in particular, health-care workers or household members of a sars patient have been known to be affected. but concern has been raised on other potential ways of transmission. on the question of the origin: recently a who investigation team has been authorised by the chinese government to travel to guangdong province. scientists currently speculate that the sars virus either jumped to humans from an animal species or mutated into a more virulent form. in its continuing work, the who team is expected to visit foshan city, where the first case of sars was reported. on the question of numbers in the european union, all 15 member states have reported to the commission a total of 46 cases - 19 probable and 27 suspected - with no deaths. it is also important to note that there has been no local transmission within the european union. in the candidate countries, efta and other european countries, 14 countries have reported data, a total of eight cases - three probable and five suspected - with no deaths. in the other countries, to date a total of 2396 cases have been reported, including 89 deaths. the unknown factors combined with the global spread of this disease have inevitably prompted extensive media attention. however, we should not lose sight of the fact that although sars is often referred to as a ‘killer pneumonia’, estimates indicate that it kills fewer people than ‘normal’ influenza. sars, however, demonstrates very clearly that we are living in a truly global environment, where the increasing mobility of people also enables diseases to move ever more freely. because of the ease and extent of modern travel, an increasing level of preparedness is required across borders to deal with the threat posed by communicable diseases. in the european union, surveillance and coordination at community level need to be strengthened to address the threat to public health. i have been stressing this need for some time now, and in the european convention, the report prepared by mr katiforis has recognised this and i hope the convention will take this up in its discussions. the eu communicable diseases network started its work three years ago to detect and control communicable diseases in people, irrespective of the cause and means of transmission. this network serves to survey and investigate the outbreaks. this also involves identifying the cause and defining control measures. the commission’s role is to coordinate and support these activities. this sars outbreak puts to the test the real capacities of the two pillars of the network – epidemiological surveillance and early warning. the network committee has, together with the commission, defined and put into operation an effective surveillance system. this system picks up all suspected sars cases and gives a complete and clear picture of developments during the outbreak. obviously we have to be cautious, and err on the side of safety. this approach seems to be working: most of the suspected cases turn out to be something else. however, this does not give grounds for complacency. the european union surveillance strategy on sars is fully connected to the global surveillance coordinated by the world health organisation. the second element of this strategy is prevention. we must work together to reduce exposure to the disease. unnecessary travel to affected areas should be discouraged or postponed. hong kong and the guangdong province of china have been identified in this respect by the who. this is under constant review and further advice will be issued if the situation in other regions warrants travel restrictions. similarly, all would agree on the importance of health screening on departure from the affected areas and the provision of information to passengers and flight crews. the commission is playing its role of coordinator, and encouraging common approaches and criteria. during the last three weeks my services have tried to integrate national measures with global ones, through regular meetings, audio-conferences and consultations with the member states, candidate countries and the who. sars, of course, entails other dimensions in addition to public health implications. the sars outbreak has already made a political and economic impact. travel advice has had an impact on air travel and tourism in asia. now, industry exhibitions and meetings have been postponed and it is predicted that asia’s economic growth may be affected. obviously, earlier notifications to the who by those affected could have mitigated many of the effects. this is a key lesson for the future. i must stress that the capacity of the commission to extend its coordinating and facilitating role any further is currently at its very limit. in the absence of new arrangements to pool the existing expertise we will not be able to go beyond our current efforts. i have referred on many occasions to our plans to strengthen our capacity to deal with communicable diseases. in my view, the most effective way to strengthen community activities is to set up a european centre for disease prevention and control. as many of you will be aware, we are well advanced in the preparation of the enabling legislation which i intend to table in the next couple of months. my proposal will be to establish such a centre by 2005. the centre will enhance surveillance. it will coordinate and facilitate common responses, and collaborate with member states, third countries and international organisations, in particular the who. it will not replace existing national capacities, but rather hook them up to act as a reference and coordination point both in routine and crisis situations. this will also play an important role in an enlarged europe. on a multinational level the sars situation can be said to be under control, but not improving, as had initially been expected. in europe the situation still appears to be manageable. however, the strict control procedures will have to continue. in the fight to beat this disease it is crucial for anybody who believes they have the symptoms and have travelled in the affected areas to consult their doctor. we must not neglect the support that the eu and its member states can give to the affected countries in their search for the cause and the remedy. there is still an ongoing discussion whether the responsible agent is close to the common cold or coronavirus. we must continue to support the who in its endeavours in this regard. finally, i can assure you that the commission will continue with the member states, and in close collaboration with the candidate countries and the who, to do everything within its powers to defeat the spread of sars. in response to what mr de rossa said earlier, i can say that there have been preliminary discussions with the council to organise a meeting of the council in the near future to discuss this issue further.

commission. – as concerns the first strand of the question, that is whether echo’s office in amman is adequate for the current needs of the region, i would like in the first place to clarify the following. the echo office in amman is the regional hub for the iraq crisis. this office has recently expanded and now has seven expatriate technical assistants and 10 local staff positions. it covers iraq and the rest of the middle east. there is also an antenna in jerusalem consisting of one expatriate technical assistant and three local-official positions. amman was selected as regional hub for this crisis because this office has adequate human and logistic resources to respond immediately to the new needs in the field. the technical assistant's role is to assess the situation on the ground, analyse the needs and make recommendations to echo. once aid is approved, the technical assistant monitors its implementation on the ground. the technical assistant also coordinates with other donors and humanitarian stakeholders. it must, however, be emphasised that echo is not an implementing organisation. the actual delivery of humanitarian aid is undertaken by echo's partners. these are international humanitarian organisations, such as the red cross, un agencies and european humanitarian ngos. regular monitoring visits were carried out before the crisis. three missions from headquarters and the field have visited iraq since january this year. the main aim of these visits was to prepare for the consequences of what was then a potential crisis. such visits have now been suspended. echo technical assistants are currently following the crisis from amman. echo will restart needs assessment and monitoring missions as soon as security conditions allow. echo will then reassess the need to further strengthen its presence on the ground. for the time being, however, echo sees its presence as adequate. as for the viability of a permanent structure in iraq and in the region, i can already say that, as was done with afghanistan, echo intends to open an office in baghdad as soon as the security situation improves. this office will be answerable to the regional office in amman. it is possible that some personnel will be transferred from amman to baghdad. echo also envisages opening an office in iran if there are large movements of refugees there. echo amman is ready to provide operational, logistic and administrative back-up for the future echo antenna in baghdad in the form of staff, equipment, assistance and so on at the outset of a presence there. as regards the evaluation of echo's activities, i would like to recall, in the first place, that an independent broader evaluation of echo's functioning carried out in 1999 stated that 'echo is currently financing the delivery of humanitarian assistance at least as well as any other organisation, and probably better and in a more cost-efficient manner than any other comparable international organisation'. there were also a number of recommendations and specific critical points in this evaluation and we have followed up very actively on the evaluation. we do this with a view to improving the overall quality of echo's management of activities, also including the verification of the results. i would like to mention the main ones. first of all, echo has introduced the logical framework approach and promoted the use of standardised performance indicators, to better measure the results and evaluate the impact of its activities wherever possible. this will also stimulate an improvement of the project proposals we get from our implementing partners and we can already see clearly this effect. echo has in parallel increased the supervision and the technical coordination of all the financed activities, notably at field level, by increasing the technical assistance capacity and creating regional support offices, as i just explained regarding the situation in amman, and also working towards a more standardised basic approach in each sector of intervention, especially in the area of health support. another step forward in the improvement of our performance based on lessons learned was the establishment of strategic programming dialogues in order to strengthen cooperation and strategies at operational and policy level. since 2000, an extensive ever-improving strategic dialogue has been taking place with all major echo partners: un agencies, ngos and other international organisations. echo has furthermore given increased priority and now prepares better for the interfaces of linking rehabilitation, relief, development and so on, playing a more proactive role, calling for coordination meetings with relevant commission services and other donors, both at field and headquarters levels. projects are earmarked with aid phases identifying those operations which can possibly be handed over to development donors, and this whole effort has been quite successful. if we look at east timor, kosovo and even afghanistan, this gradual handing over has been better than in the case of previous conflicts. in parallel with the introduction of these key elements for improving performance, every year echo now presents an evaluation plan by the start of the new budgetary year. evaluations are thus synchronised with the planning and implementation of all stages of echo's operations. evaluations focus on country operations, on partners and thematic issues. the evaluation plan ensures, on a two-yearly basis, that all major operations are now being evaluated. a programme of evaluation using external consultants, and focused on echo operations, partners' capacity as well as on specific thematic issues, is therefore ongoing. of particular relevance are the recent evaluations of the unhcr and the world food programme, major international partners which also play a major role in the present crisis in iraq. the evaluation reports are periodically published on echo's website, once member states have been informed. lastly, it should be mentioned that echo has also undertaken the implementation of the commission reform programme. this has positively influenced all administrative and financial aspects of the commission's work. echo is today in a totally different situation compared to the situation when this commission came into office. a recent article in european voice made me think that what was promised by me in the hearing in parliament in august 1999 has been delivered. echo is today, for good reason, a respected player in the game of international humanitarian aid. coming to the last part of the question, as regards the existence of an agreement with the united nations for tackling 'the day after' in iraq, i recall what the european council stated on 21 march, that the un should play a central role during and after the current crisis. my view here is simply that the un system has a unique – i repeat: unique – legitimacy, mandate, capacity and practical experience in coordinating assistance in post-conflict situations. that is where that discussion should start.

justified in view of the seriousness of the recent events. at this stage, and in full agreement with the council, it is proposed to include and develop three guidelines within this framework. first, effect at regional and even local level, in the general interest of the union and for the benefit of all our citizens. commission. – mr president, i wish to begin by welcoming our new colleagues from the new member states. it is a real pleasure to see them in the european parliament and i welcome them to the eu family. firstly, let me thank the rapporteur, mr manders, for his report concerning the commission's proposal on environmental liability. environmental liability is an important subject that has received well-deserved attention and caused intensive discussion for many years. the commission has been working on this issue for a long time, in close contact with the parties concerned and civil society. this process has re-emphasised the strategic importance of the underlying principles, whilst also pointing to a great diversity of opinions on the details of implementation. one is tempted to say that there are almost as many different views on the main issues as there are parties involved. i am thus well aware that this proposal is a complex and sensitive one. difficult choices had to be made on many of its aspects and the appropriate balance had to be found among competing interests. we believe that the commission succeeded in reaching this balance when it adopted the proposal in january 2002. it is with the aim of maintaining, if not further improving, this balance that it will consider the amendments adopted by parliament. let me briefly present to you the main features of the commission's proposal. the proposal aims to establish a community framework whereby environmental damage – which is defined in the proposal as biodiversity damage, water damage and land damage – would be prevented or remedied through a system of environmental liability. whenever possible the operator who has caused the environmental damage – or provoked an imminent threat of such damage occurring – must, in accordance with the polluter pays principle, bear the costs associated with the implementation of the necessary preventive or restorative measures. in certain cases, in which no operator can be held liable or a liable operator is unable to pay, member states must assume the responsibility for finding an alternative source of financing the measures in question. there are several key issues that deserve special attention. these issues certainly invite more detailed comments, but today i will be as concise as possible. firstly, the scope of the proposal in terms of the activities and biodiversity to be covered: in the commission's view, strict liability should apply to the activities listed in annex i to the proposal, and also to occupational activities other than those listed in annex i, it being understood that this second tier of liability is fault-based. the commission considers that suppressing this part of the liability regime is unacceptable since this would weaken the proposal. conversely, the commission does not believe it either justifiable or workable to expand strict liability to all occupational activities in the eu. having commented on the scope, let me just finish by saying that the debate on the amendments will be an extremely important one, during which i am sure we will hear some new arguments.
the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy has adopted a number of amendments to the proposal. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we are discussing today a draft directive which we have been waiting for for 20 years. the practical application of the polluter pays principle seems to be more complex than we thought. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the environment is protected, and that the environment is protected in a way that is not harmful to the environment. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's environmental policy is not distorted by the introduction of new technologies, and that the community's environmental policy is not distorted by the introduction of new technologies. i am very pleased that the commission has taken the necessary steps to ensure that the directive is implemented in a way that is consistent with the principles of the treaty of rome. in particular, biodiversity as defined in the plan is limited to the habitats and species covered by the habitats and birds directives, i.e. only 13% of the territory of the european union. secondly, the definition of environmental damage must be broadened to include radiation, damage to air quality and damage to biodiversity from genetically modified organisms. thirdly, the areas of marine and nuclear pollution are not covered. we are told that there are international conventions. however, these usually cover traditional damage and not the concept of environmental damage. moreover, they have not been signed by several member states of the european union. and yet they contain clauses expressly prohibiting the introduction of provisions for extended environmental liability. the directive must therefore be clear and explicit about the current liability regime and also provide for the possibility of amending these international treaties, and we should await the commission's proposals in this respect. in addition, exemptions from environmental liability are provided for emissions or activities which have been authorised or which were not considered harmful at the time of authorisation. it's called "permit and state of the art defences". i believe that these exceptions undermine the soundness of the objectives of the directive, limit the scope of the liability regime, undermine the 'polluter pays' principle. there is a study carried out by the commission itself, commissioner, which shows that 10 out of the 15 member states of the union do not provide for such exemptions. the new directive cannot therefore lead many member states to relax the strictness of their environmental legislation. the proposal for a directive establishes a public law regime under which the competent authority is responsible for the definition and implementation of appropriate preventive or remedial measures. but this should not mean that the burden falls on the taxpayer. because there's a danger of us ending up there. the primary responsibility for prevention and rehabilitation should therefore lie with the operator. the competent public authority must follow the procedure for finding and recovering the damage. there is also the issue of indirect and only indirect access to justice for citizens. the directive does not provide for the possibility of citizens having recourse directly to the courts. and i think that is where the aarhus treaty is being violated. i also believe that there should be a compulsory system of insurance for operators with common rules on financial guarantees. if that is the case, then competition will not be distorted. on the contrary, if it is not there, it may be distorted, and the prevention system will not be strong, and i think there will not be the beneficial effects on the economy that we would expect. the committee on the environment, which i have the honour of chairing, has adopted an opinion in the spirit of these observations. we are now submitting to the house, together with many other colleagues from many political groups, a series of proposals with less ambition but which are more conciliatory. we are trying to get closer to the council's positions so that we can see the greek presidency reaching a political agreement at the environment council on 13 june. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the ecosystem and the flow of matter and energy have predictable, describable paths. human activity must adapt to them. we don't protect nature just by putting a fence around it. to protect the viability of europe, we need a green turn in industry and the whole economy. we cannot say that we are not for one or the other. i hope that the results of our vote will send a clear political message throughout europe: that we are determined to develop a genuine policy to ensure better protection of the environment, compatible with the social and economic objectives of the union. our vote is not going to make any immediate change. if we vote for the amendments which we have the honour to table, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i think we can open a new path which will eventually establish a model of sustainability and responsibility in europe and beyond.
the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment is a very ambitious one, and it aims to minimise environmental damage both by means of preventive measures and by allocating the cost of repairing the damage. the amendments we support are the necessary compromises not only to avoid the adoption of the directive but also to make the whole protection system sustainable and to avoid market distortions. i congratulate mr manders and mr papayannakis on having been able to make the necessary compromises. the implementation of the 'polluter pays' principle is of fundamental importance. it is a question of the need to develop the european union's policy on the environment, and it is a question of the need to develop the european union's policy on the environment. the compulsory provision of financial guarantees to make good environmental damage is a conditio sine qua non for the effective protection of the environment. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work is a very good one. however, the introduction of compulsory insurance must be gradual in cooperation with the parties concerned. it should be borne in mind that insurance companies need some time to prepare. in any event, the phases of introduction of the compulsory insurance scheme must be defined in the text of the directive, with corresponding specification of the type of damage to be covered and the activities to be covered. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the environmental impact of the use of the land is not affected by the pollution caused by the use of the land. otherwise the final financial burden will be shifted to the taxpayer. the pursuit of activities for which a licence exists and which are not considered harmful at the time of their pursuit should not exclude the operator's liability, but the existence of a licence or the failure to detect in time the harmful effects of the activity in question could act as mitigating circumstances when the costs of restoring the ecological damage are charged to the operator, provided that the latter has fully complied with the conditions imposed by the applicable legislation or its licence in the course of its activity. the criteria for the differentiation of the compensation coverage, which indirectly indicate the size of the undertaking which ensures that the viability of small undertakings is not jeopardised, are accepted. the above also shows that, in order to protect the environment effectively and to prevent ecological disasters, the activities falling within the scope of the directive should be reviewed periodically taking into account the latest scientific findings and the experience gained in the meantime.

council mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is a great pleasure to be with you today to present the results of the council's work on severe acute respiratory syndrome to date. as you know, the presidency convened an emergency council meeting on 6 may to discuss this serious matter which, in addition to the obvious and significant effects on public health and the economy, raises legitimate concerns among citizens, often exacerbated by the way in which the matter is presented in the media. before i tell you the results of the council, let me make a preliminary comment. the case of severe acute respiratory syndrome shows once again that infectious diseases, like many other problems affecting public health, i mention bioterrorism as another example, go far beyond the level of the member states and constitute the need for institutional changes that will make health protection a key priority of a united europe. this perspective will further facilitate coordination on prevention, control and early intervention to combat diseases, both in the community and internationally. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i am convinced, mr president, that europe is the best way to promote in each of our countries ambitious public health policies, particularly in the field of disease prevention and control. in today's europe, and particularly in the enlargement europe, health must gain a firm and strong legal basis, allowing for immediate, coordinated, scientifically sound and effective interventions. i would now like to inform you of the results of the work of the extraordinary council. i would remind you that the council meeting on 6 may brought together for the first time the ministers for health of the acceding countries, as well as mrs brundtland, director-general of the who, to inform us of the current developments in the world in the field of atypical pneumonia. as for the scientific epidemiological aspect of the problem, according to the experts of the international organizations, we know in brief that the cause of the syndrome is an unrecognized until the recent appearance of the virus belonging to the category of coronaviruses. its molecular identification was accomplished in a very short time, considering how long it took to identify the hiv virus of aids. despite its identification, we still don't know its exact natural history, as we still don't have specific antiviral drugs to treat it, nor are we anywhere near a vaccine to prevent it. as for the mode of transmission, there is strong evidence that it is transmitted by close contact, most likely via droplets. there is no evidence that the goods arriving in the european union from the virus-infected areas pose a risk to public health. in terms of epidemiology, confirmed or suspected cases in european union countries are limited and patients have been effectively isolated and treated. so far, the further spread of infection has been prevented and, most importantly, we have no fatal cases. the council held a full and constructive exchange of views with mrs brundtland and noted that the world health assembly next week would be an excellent opportunity to reassess the world situation and assess efforts to deal with it. as regards the community's measures to deal with the problem, i would first of all point out that the implementation of health protection measures is a matter for the authorities of the member states. a network for the epidemiological surveillance and control of communicable diseases is already in operation at community level and is responsible for coordinating the measures. the network proved to be an effective means of exchanging information, in which the acceding countries also participated fully. the council endorsed the guidelines agreed on 10 april 2003 by the monitoring network committee, which i summarise as follows: - rapid detection of all suspected cases through good surveillance, - protection of persons at risk of infection through effective isolation in hospitals, with particular emphasis on taking measures to protect nursing staff, - special focus of measures on air travel, which appears to be a major contributor to the spread of the syndrome, mainly through standardised screening of passengers departing from affected areas, through advice provided to passengers on board aircraft and, finally, through information at arrival airports. these measures must be applied in all member states. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the programme. the council decided that community action and efforts through the communicable disease monitoring network and the new programme in the field of public health should be continued. cooperation between the member states, the commission and the world health organization should also be continued in order to prevent and eventually eradicate this atypical pneumonia. this cooperation should be directed mainly to providing assistance to the affected areas and to developing diagnostic tests to promote research for the manufacture and supply of vaccines in sufficient quantities. the council also urged the member states and the acceding countries to implement fully all the guidelines of the monitoring network, to contribute actively to the establishment of a special group of experts on severe acute respiratory syndrome under the monitoring network committee and to provide the commission with all information by 15 may on the measures taken to combat the syndrome. finally, i would like to note that we have asked the commission to continue coordinating the actions of the member states and to review the guidelines for the monitoring network on a regular basis. the council will review the situation and developments at its meeting on 2 june, at which time the commission will report on the measures taken by the member states. on the basis of this report, the council will take further action if deemed necessary. it also supports the commission's intention to present the first draft proposal for the establishment of a european centre for disease prevention and control. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have confined myself to this summary of the council's work and i am at your disposal to answer your questions.

in writing. - (el) this directive on an environmental liability system is based on the basic principle of the polluter-pays principle. this principle has proved effective in requiring those responsible to make good environmental damage, but it has also proved detrimental in weakening effective prevention and has proved to be the most cynical alibi for increasing the tax burden on 'polluted citizens' - polluters (large companies) no longer paying for the disasters they cause (erika, prestige, sevezo etc.) and further reinforced by incentives and tax breaks. environmental damage is reduced to blatant hypocrisy, in that the 'financial guarantees' on the operator are shifted to the state and the workers either by increasing the operating costs or by passing them on to the price of the products. given the exemptions and its limited scope, this directive is reduced to a 'vine leaf' hiding the interests of monopolies, insofar as it does not include the overall protection of biodiversity, pollution by hydrocarbons, nuclear damage, non-ionizing radiation, gmos, etc. and it exempts from all responsibility, in a provocative way, those who cause enormous environmental disasters by carrying out barbaric and unprovoked military interventions. the limited definitions of damage, liability and other basic concepts, with their exceptions and curious "presumptions of non-liability", lead us to adopt a particularly cautious and critical attitude towards this "environmental liability".

now, as to the sequence of extradition requests in relation to the european arrest warrant. the draft extradition agreement leaves each member state free to choose to which country to extradite a person. i would remind you that when we discussed and agreed on the european arrest warrant within the european union, the idea that the arrest warrant issued by one member state should precede any extradition request to any other third country was not accepted. but even if we decide in our own internal procedures in the future to give such priority to the european arrest warrant, the draft agreement contains a specific provision which facilitates us in such a decision. in particular, it recognises that future developments in the european union may have an impact on the application of the agreement and provides for a review of the agreement in the light of these developments. i would like to reiterate that, in the draft extradition agreement, each member state has the option of council mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the prospect of completing the enlargement process with the 10 new member states has led, since last year, to a new reflection on the european union's relations with its new geographical and political environment, its new neighbours. in essence, beyond the name issues, what emerges is a new vision of how the european union should see the future of its relations with a number of countries around it. this reflection, called 'wider europe - new neighbourhood', was launched last year with the intervention and contributions of the member states. i refer to the letter from jack straw, mrs lindh and mr pagrotsky, the minister for trade, and then to a joint letter from mr solana and mr patten. the council discussed and adopted conclusions on the new neighbourhood initiative on 19 december 2002 for ukraine, moldova and belarus and called for concrete proposals for the project, extending its scope to other neighbouring regions. in this way, the council expressed its intention to develop an ambitious, long-term and integrated approach for each of these three neighbouring countries. this approach is based on the principle of differentiation, taking into account the specific circumstances of each country, its political and economic potential, its performance and the union's objectives for each country. today, almost a year after it began, the completion of the enlargement process has strengthened the prospect of such an approach, as it sets out the wider context of the union's relations with its neighbours, thus achieving the spread of core values such as peace, security and prosperity, which are of immense importance to the citizens of the union. the combination of such a policy with the continuation and deepening of enlargement is intended to create a ring of friends around the european union. the copenhagen council spoke of common political and economic values, of avoiding the creation of new dividing lines and of promoting peace and stability within and beyond the union's borders. these were the main points discussed in april, when the strengthening of cooperation between the european union and its eastern and mediterranean neighbours and the way in which their progress could be assessed were discussed. the same issue was discussed at the european conference of heads opportunity to begin a dialogue on the general principles of the whole initiative and to adopt a declaration specifying its common objectives, objectives accepted by the new member states, accepted by in writing. - (el) the new proposal for a directive differs significantly from the idea which has been put forward so far in the fight against foot-and-mouth disease and is moving in the right direction. the most fundamental difference is the authorisation of vaccines as the first measure to combat foot-and-mouth disease, whereas the measures of isolation, transport ban and slaughter, which were until now the only measures authorised, are now considered as additional measures. at the same time, the proposal provides for the marginalisation of countries where the disease appears and requires greater veterinary control and more staff with the necessary flexibility. however, we oppose the provision which allows the european commission to decide on vaccines or to refer the matter to a community body to take a decision itself, even without the agreement of the member state concerned. member states and the competent national services are the only competent authorities to assess the problem and decide on the necessary measures.

commission. – mr president, the commission's overall policy towards vietnam is to encourage and support continued progress on human rights and democratisation and to raise concerns where abuses occur or where a deterioration in the situation becomes evident. the commission works closely with eu member states in monitoring human rights developments in the country and participates in all démarches to the government of vietnam on human rights issues. i can assure honourable members that the commission and eu member states have repeatedly urged the government of vietnam to strengthen its respect for political and religious freedoms and to further strengthen economic and social freedoms. article 1 of the european community and vietnam cooperation agreement of 1995 states that respect for human rights and democratic principles is the basis of our cooperation. this reference has given the commission increased possibilities to discuss human rights issues with vietnam, for example in joint committee meetings held under the agreement. with the aim of encouraging and supporting the continued commitment of the government of vietnam to human rights issues, the commission is currently considering proposing a further reinforcement of the relations in this field. this could be done through the establishment of a mechanism for a structured human rights dialogue, taking account of the experience gained with dialogues that the eu has already established with other countries. let me recall that the constitution of vietnam guarantees freedom of belief and religion and that the vietnamese government officially recognises six religions. the constitution also specifies that it is forbidden to violate freedom of belief or religion or to take advantage of it, or to act against the laws or policies of the state. this provision is attributed to the desire of the vietnamese authorities to control the pace of change and to maintain cohesion in their society during the process of transition to a market economy. however, it may also be used against non-approved religious groups which, according to the vietnamese authorities, engage in political activities or are potential elements of disunity. reports of harassment of christians in vietnam, especially the montagnards and hmong christians, have increased since the violent uprising in the central highlands in 2001, in which some religious groups were reportedly implicated. a number of so far unconfirmed reports since then have alleged repeated actions by local official forces aimed at forcing highlanders to renounce their faith. commission president prodi and commissioner patten discussed the situation in the central highlands with vietnam's prime minister, phan van khai, during his visit to the commission last september. they agreed that the commission would explore, under its financial cooperation programme, specific activities involving, inter alia, ethnic minorities to reduce poverty in the central highlands and thus to deal with some of the root causes of problems in the area. a preparatory mission of experts is currently in the field. as mr dupuis has already mentioned, recent, promising, positive signals have been sent out by the vietnamese government regarding the still unrecognised unified buddhist church of vietnam. there has been a meeting between prime minister phan van khai and the supreme patriarch, the venerable thich huyen quang. a meeting between the patriarch and the venerable thich quang do, another prominent leader of the unified buddhist church, has also been authorised. although no change with regard to the church's legal status has so far taken place, we believe that these events, as mentioned, are encouraging steps towards enhanced tolerance of religious freedom in vietnam. let me conclude by emphasising that i am convinced that what is needed in vietnam is continued and more rapid progress in the country's reform programme so that the administration would learn to deal with a wider range of use and appreciate the value of accommodating dissent in the system of government. i thank all honourable members of the european parliament for their very valuable and good speeches. commission. the commission has taken a proactive and leading role in responding to the outbreak of severe acute respiratory syndrome (sars). as recently stated by the council on sars on 6 may 2003, this has been undertaken through the eu network for the epidemiological surveillance and control of communicable diseases in the community, working in the framework of decision no 2119/1998/ec. this has provided a very effective basis for the rapid exchange of information within the eu and for a coordinated response in which efta and candidate countries have fully participated in collaboration with the who. at its extraordinary meeting on sars, the council broadly agreed the orientation developed by the commission with the assistance of the network committee. although the application of health protection measures falls to the authorities of the member states, the orientation for immediate and future actions will focus on the following issues: rapid detection of all suspect cases of sars through good surveillance; protection of those at risk of infection through effective isolation of sars patients in hospitals, including measures to protect carers; particular attention to be paid to air travel, which has been an important factor in the spread of sars, notably to standardised screening of passengers leaving affected areas; on-board advice to passengers and effective information at ports of entry from affected areas; raising awareness among professionals and the public and the timely and accurate reporting and sharing of information with other countries, in particular eea and efta countries, acceding and candidate countries, and with the who. cooperation should also be developed with other partners such as airline companies, and the organising bodies of mass gatherings. the council also took note of the commission's intention to submit a proposal to create a european centre for disease prevention and control.

the commission. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the directive is implemented in greece and has recently notified the commission of the implementing legislation. the commission is currently in the process of evaluating the transfer and will take a decision after a careful examination of the file. however, it is clear that, according to clause 5 of the directive, member states must adopt measures to prevent the abuse which may result from the use of successive fixedterm contracts. the directive provides some options for member states in applying the clause. they shall lay down at least one of the following measures: objective reasons justifying the renewal of fixed-term contracts, maximum total duration of contracts and number of renewals. a first reading of the presidential decree shows that article 5 provides for the above, and that it expressly states that the renewal of fixed-term employment contracts is permissible if justified by an objective reason, and indicates examples of cases of assistance of an objective reason. of course, it is for the member states themselves to define what is meant by the phrase 'objective reasons'. however, the measures adopted must be sufficient to prevent abuse. for example, the argument that employment in the public sector is in itself an objective reason for successive indefinite fixed-term contracts cannot be accepted. there should be an objective justification based on the nature of the object. the commission, as i said, intends to assess the transposition of the implementing legislation and to take further action if necessary.

in writing. - (el) the report is correct in commenting on the dangers facing small-scale fishing (which accounts for 75% of community fishing vessels) with the implementation of the new common fisheries policy, which will result in the loss of 28 000 jobs, economic stagnation and desertification of coastal areas. but the report does not question the policy that is producing the difficulties it is only describing. on the contrary, it regards them as a fact and is only interested in moderating their consequences, slowing down the rate at which they occur and 'controlling' losses. the rapporteur is under no illusions about the commission's intentions and calls on the commission to examine its options. we don't have that kind of illusion. the fisheries policy as it is applied and the proposed policy, as it stands or with some amendments, prove that the eu is on the path of entrusting the exploitation of fisheries resources to large companies. this is the direction taken by the financing measures for the demolition of small and medium-sized fishing vessels in order to eliminate small and medium-sized fishermen and further strengthen the fishing capacity of large vessels. the situation cannot be reversed by means of wish lists and appeals to the goodwill of the commission. only the fishermen themselves and their fight can overturn these policies and prevent their extermination.
in writing. - (el) i voted in favour of the rothley report, despite the fact that the amendments proposed by the gue/ngl, the greens and the liberals were rejected yesterday, for the reasons stated by mr cox. this is clearly an insufficient step towards transparency and the settlement of a problem which is an affront to the european parliament. the amendment proposed by the socialist group to delete paragraph 5 referring to the bureau's decision on travel expenses, etc. raises questions about the real intentions of the european parliament and, to say the least, causes confusion.
in writing. - (el) i voted in favour because, following the sinking of the prestige off the spanish coast and the enormous ecological disaster, immediate protection against single-hull oil tankers is needed by imposing an immediate timetable for their withdrawal from circulation. the governments of the fifteen should support these measures and ignore the pressure exerted by any shipowner who, out of self-interest, is opposed to the necessary regulations to protect the seas and beaches.
the european parliament, on behalf of the new democracy meps, in writing. - (el) our position in the final vote on the piecyk report was to abstain. we understand, of course, that the purpose of the withdrawal of single-hull oil tankers is to protect the environment by preventing further dramatic accidents at sea. we are of course in favour of this objective, as we have shown by voting in favour of all previous reports on the subject. but these final provisions seem to be the result of a political reaction, in the heat of the action, to the sinking of the prestige. this also explains the eagerness to see the eu move forward independently of the who, whereas everyone knows that in the field of maritime transport, which goes beyond european borders, international solutions are preferable. this is all the more so as the previous withdrawal schedule is not yet applicable. we therefore do not believe that the consequences of these provisions on the competitiveness of the economy have been seriously considered. in particular, greek shipping is hit hard, to the detriment of workers in the sector. by abstaining we express our deep scepticism of the position of the council of ministers and, more importantly, of the greek presidency, which should approach the problem with more coolness, especially as we greeks have more experience of these problems and our economy is more affected by these provisions.
in writing. - (el) the safety of ships, crews and the environment is an issue which cannot be addressed by piecemeal measures, however important, such as the mandatory double hull precondition for oil tankers calling at ports in the member states. a genuine safety policy must tackle the lack of responsibility on the part of shipowners, apply substantial measures against breaches of legislation, adjust operational positions to today's increased requirements and contribute to improving the living and working conditions of crews by safeguarding their rights and empowering their unions to intervene decisively. any provision must be introduced in the framework of the imo and the ilo, which should play a vital role in international shipping, while rejecting the philosophy of compromise with the interests of shipping. a typical example of how these interests are served at the expense of the environment is in the long transition periods, without any real justification in terms of security of supply, and in the exemption from double hull requirements for vessels over 500 to 600 tonnes. the eu promotes the absence of liability of shipowners in the best possible way. one example: the ship repair industry in greece, a country with one of the largest fleets in the world, has been virtually wiped out. only a determined struggle by the workers, the seamen and the regions concerned, especially the coastal regions, can achieve positive results against this policy.

council - the special council on employment, social policy, health and consumers of 6 may 2003 adopted conclusions in which, after a careful examination of the situation regarding severe acute respiratory syndrome both within the european union and worldwide, and the various measures taken to deal with it, it was confirmed that it is of great importance to establish the situation quickly and to consider future actions. the council considers that the community epidemiological surveillance and control network for communicable diseases has proved to be a very effective basis for rapid information exchange within the union and for a coordinated response in which the acceding countries have been fully involved. the council, having recalled that the implementation of health protection measures falls within the competence of the authorities of the member states, confirmed the benefits of effective coordination of these measures through the committee of the epidemiological monitoring network. it also supported the guidelines for immediate and future actions agreed on 10 april by the epidemiological monitoring network committee, which are as follows: - rapid detection of all suspected sars cases through good surveillance, - protection of those at risk of infection from patients through effective isolation of sars cases in hospitals, including measures to protect nursing staff, - air travel, which has been a significant factor in the spread of sars, needs to be given special attention, in particular through standardised screening of passengers departing from affected areas, by providing advice to passengers on board aircraft and effective information to arriving airports from affected areas, - vigilance of both professionals and the general public and timely and accurate transfer of information from and to the who and other countries of arrival and departure, and in particular to the eea/eea countries and other countries of destination, are also of particular importance. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the future of the european union. the council encouraged the member states and the acceding countries to fully implement the guidelines for immediate and future action of the monitoring network committee and to actively contribute to the establishment of a dedicated sars expert group under the monitoring network committee with a view to developing common ways and advice on health measures across europe. the council further stressed the need for continued cooperation between the member states, the commission and who and called on the member states to ensure, inter alia:- the rapid and effective diagnosis of suspected and potential sars cases and their appropriate isolation in hospitals,- the appropriate protection of nursing staff dealing with these patients,- the provision of guidance and information to nursing staff and the public,- measures that are consistent across the union, for the provision and collection of information and traceability from international travellers arriving from affected areas or international travellers departing from such areas,- the timely and accurate reporting and exchange of information with the who, the commission, air carriers and other countries. finally, the council encouraged the commission to continue to coordinate union action against sars, to review regularly the guidelines for immediate and future action, in particular in the light of advice from who, to consider the possible development of a general preparedness plan for communicable diseases and health threats, to coordinate and network the knowledge and experience of national laboratories, and to financially support research and development of validated diagnostic tests, therapeutic interventions and vaccines. the council reviewed the situation and developments at its meeting of 2 june 2003, took note of the commission's progress report on the latest developments in relation to sars and exchanged views on the current situation. all member states welcomed the commission's report and the initiatives already taken or planned in this field. the presidency stressed the importance of coordinating the exchange of information at european level, given the cross-border nature of sars.

in writing. -el) the commission proposal follows the 1992 revision and remains true to the philosophy of reducing intervention prices by 5.9% and of partially compensating for these reductions by direct aid to the surface. it serves the interests of the wheat trade and processing industries by guaranteeing them cheap raw materials. at the same time, the incomes of wheat producers are revised downwards, as the compensation is 50% and not 100%, prices and compensation remain constant and are not adjusted on the basis of average community inflation and, finally, the average intervention price is reduced through the proposal to abolish the monthly increases in the intervention price. the amendments proposed by the rapporteur of the european parliament are more positive than the commission's proposals, with the exception of the reference to durum wheat, which is however subject to different regulations. in substance, however, they are moving in the same direction as the commission's proposal and differ only on quantitative elements, without contesting anything and without proposing measures which would go against the basic philosophy of the commission. despite the relevance of its conclusions, this makes the report less effective and serves only as a veneer for a policy which favours the interests of multinational companies to the detriment of small and mediumsized farms.
in writing. -el) the aim of the commission's proposal is to reduce community production and increase imports from third countries. in the union and greece, rice is grown on pathogenic land for which it is difficult to find an alternative solution. we therefore consider the proposed quota of 203 000 hectares for greece to be unacceptable, which is less than the previous quota which we have more than covered. the proposed measures reduce the incomes of rice producers while increasing the profits of traders, who will buy their raw materials at ridiculous prices, since intervention prices will have a proportional impact on trade prices without compensating for these reductions, despite the commission's claims to the contrary. these allegations are also unfounded, since the compensation rate is calculated on the basis of the difference between the intervention price before revision and the private storage price after revision. although more positive, the rapporteur's amendments are in the wrong in relation to his objective conclusions on the state of the sector. the rapporteur rejects the abolition of intervention but accepts the draconian reduction of intervention prices by 50%, which in practice amounts to their abolition. it confirms the problem of the abundance of imports, but does not differ from the quotas proposed by the commission. apart from the fact that its proposals exacerbate the situation rather than significantly improving it, this is why we will not vote in favour of the report.
in writing. - (el) the proposals on the dairy sector perpetuate the unfair treatment of countries such as greece by keeping quotas at unacceptably low levels, exacerbating their dependence on dairy products and ruining producers through high coresponsibility levies due to the outrageously low quotas allocated to them. the eu prefers to increase intervention by removing surplus milk products from over-saturated markets, mainly in the northern countries, rather than directing the money spent on intervention towards meeting the needs of countries such as greece, which cannot even cover half of their domestic demand. it is scandalous that the quotas granted in compensation for the reduction in guide prices are increased in a higher proportion in the more developed countries than in the others. the proposals foresee an increase in quotas for greece of between 6 000 and 14 000 tonnes, while the increase for the netherlands is between 335 000 and 110 000 tonnes. the national livestock sector is doomed to stagnation and greeks are forced to consume imported pasteurised products because fresh milk does not reach the country in time, whereas there is potential to increase production and meet demand. we are asking for a fair redistribution of quotas, based on demographic criteria, consumption requirements and production potential. that is why we will vote against these reports, which are heading in diametrically opposite directions.

in writing. the open method of coordination is a means of promoting community policies outside the framework provided for by the treaties. it consists of defining guidelines, transferring them to national policies and monitoring, evaluating and revising them. it is promoted as a voluntary coordination procedure and as a mechanism for the exchange of experience. however, the fact that it does not require any legislation at community level makes it particularly opaque and therefore ideal for promoting policies that are unfavourable to citizens or fall outside the eu's remit. from its introduction to the present day, it has been applied on many occasions to employment and social policy issues, research, business, education, immigration, asylum, etc. citizens of the eu member states are thus confronted with a flood of anti-worker measures (e.g. on industrial relations, pensions and the famous bologna process for universities), without realising that they come from the eu. the report under consideration not only fails to combat the anti-democratic nature of this procedure, but also tries to embellish it and to give it a democratic veneer. these are the reasons why the members of the greek communist party voted against the report, just as they voted against the proposal of the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport. workers will not be fooled by eu policy, no matter how big the attempt is and how the union tries to convince them.

the rapporteur. madam president, the two regulations we are discussing today are added to a series of union legislation on genetically modified organisms which concerns not only their restricted use but also their deliberate release into the environment, novel foods and novel food ingredients, the mandatory labelling of soybeans and genetically modified maize. these regulations provide a body of legislation, providing rules on the circulation and disposal of food and feed products consisting of, containing or produced from genetically modified organisms. in addition, the necessary information is given to consumers so that they are aware when they want to buy a product. so when a food is made up of, contains or is produced from genetically modified organisms, the words 'this product is made up of, contains or is produced from gmos' will be on the packaging. the council's common position supports the proposal for a regulation on which i am rapporteur, on the traceability and labelling of genetically modified organisms and products and the traceability of food and feed, and amending directive 2001/18 of the european parliament, and the commission's proposal, in particular the provisions aimed at the effective implementation of the regulation. in this way, the council is seeking, mainly on the basis of traceability, to ensure the smooth functioning of the market, a high level of consumer protection in cases where it is not possible to apply analytical methods to distinguish between conventional products and products produced from gmos with the following elements: the introduction of systems for the identification of genetically modified organisms by the issuance of a unique identifier, the obligation for undertakings to transmit information on the identity of the product, the obligation for undertakings to retain further information for at least five years. i therefore believe that the rapid adoption of this regulation without going through the conciliation procedure with the council is what we are asking for. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rules on the labelling of genetically modified organisms are applied in the member states. i would also like to stress that, as far as the question of crop blending is concerned, we are talking about food and feed here, and we are therefore calling on the european commission to develop guidelines for the coexistence of genetically modified and conventional organic crops. finally, i think it is useful to add the creation of a register - this is in the amendment - for the publication of technical guidelines on sampling and testing methods, because it enhances transparency and helps to ensure a coordinated approach and effective application of the regulation. the rapid adoption of that regulation, as well as of the regulation on genetically modified food and feed, ensures that consumers are informed about food and feed produced from genetically modified organisms so that they can choose a product after being informed in advance. this will also lead to the lifting of the de facto moratorium on the approval of new gmos and the avoidance of a trade war with the usa, canada, argentina, egypt and other countries. i am of the opinion that europe is lagging behind in these new technologies and biotechnology, as described in the council conclusions and the road map, and the importance of this development, with these two reports today and the vote tomorrow, will be important for europe, because we are significantly behind in this promising 21st century technology compared to our competitors, with negative consequences at all levels: economic, social and even environmental. i therefore propose that we proceed to the vote on these amendments, which do not change the substance of the legislative text, and therefore avoid a compromise and have these two regulations come into force as soon as possible. the problem of not being able to keep track of the speed of biotechnology development has been what has really led to the reservations, and i think it is time for the european union to move in a positive way towards this technology. i think we should proceed to vote on a text which is as close as possible to the council's positions.

mr president, it is obvious that the technical issues involved in this matter have been sufficiently analysed, so i will concentrate on the political aspect of the matter, to say that the case for a single european sky is driven by two different and quite conflicting rationales. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's air transport system is not affected by the consequences of the accident. one of the main reasons for this situation is the continuing increase in air traffic and, above all, the absence of a common airspace management system in the european countries. the other reasoning reflects the concern of some member states who would like to ensure their rights in their airspace, particularly in relation to their defence obligations and needs, and the possibility of conducting military exercises in that airspace. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the european parliament has adopted the first line of reasoning. as in many other areas of european policy, the choice of a genuine community policy and a single regulation is considered to be more efficient. that was the logic of the first reading. the council, unfortunately, relied entirely on second-guessing. worries and doubts were prevalent. the council attached particular importance to matters of public policy, security and defence. in this way, he has effectively renewed the commission's proposal and, of course, his position has nothing to do with the position of the european parliament at first reading. if the council were to agree to the objective of a single european sky, it would have to adopt a different strategy. otherwise, he would have to honestly say he disagrees with the project. it is obvious, mr president, that we are heading towards a process of reconciliation. in this process the council must show flexibility. i firmly believe that there are ways of taking substantive steps towards the single european sky without affecting national sensitivities and vital interests. where there's a will, there's always a way!

the commission is not prepared to accept this. the committee on legal affairs and the internal market has given me the honour of drawing up an own-initiative report on the legal bases and the respect for community law. the title of the report is not accurate. i'd say he's a little misleading. in fact, this is the big issue that is causing the council, the commission and the european parliament to take controversial positions and that concerns the examination of the possible legal bases for the european union's competence to provide for criminal sanctions for certain serious breaches of community law. there is a wide range of views as to whether and to what extent such an activity can be legalised. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i thank them for their contribution and i would like to inform the house that the report was based on those points where there seems to be more or less consensus. the common objective of all of us must be to implement community provisions more effectively, but with solutions that are reliable, because it is important to create legal certainty. i would also remind you that the question of criminal sanctioning of serious breaches of community law has been raised in the past in connection with legislative proposals concerning the protection of the environment, the protection of the community's financial interests, the safeguarding of intellectual property rights, pollution from ships and pollution offences in general. the matter is quite complicated from a legal point of view. the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. the report focuses on the legalization of criminal sanctions under the first pillar. in order to make the problem clear, i shall confine myself to the main question to which the report gives a positive answer, namely whether the community can impose on the member states the obligation to provide for criminal provisions for serious breaches of community law. this is the so-called mixed method, where the community imposes an obligation on the states to provide for criminal sanctions for the matter in question. we have limited ourselves to this method because it seems to have a high degree of consensus. on the other hand, the strict community method of directly providing for criminal sanctions in community law, a kind of communitization of criminal law, is faced with serious legal objections, starting from the fact that there is no clear legal basis in the treaty on this subject, that criminal sanctions are part of the national sovereignty of the member states and that criminal justice is an integral part of national culture. it is also argued that criminal sanction is linked to the restriction of individual rights, which presupposes a fully constitutionally organised state and not an imperfect legal order, with obvious economic elements and democratic deficit, such as the european union. in any event, even if the community's strict method were accepted, it would be limited to providing for a criminal penalty. the court of justice has no jurisdiction to impose a sanction in this case. the so-called national method, which means the right of the member states to provide for criminal sanctions for infringements of community law, does not create any problems. the member states are free to follow this method. the sanction must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive. it was also understood that it does not deal with the issue of the harmonisation of criminal rights and penalties for which only the third pillar can be used in specific cases. the draft constitution is taking these issues to a new level. the position of the report on the basic question we have raised above, namely whether the community can impose on the member states an obligation to provide for criminal sanctions, is that the community legislator has the legal capacity to require this from the member states. in particular, it accepts that article 10 tec lays down the principle of legality, which implies an obligation on the states to ensure that infringements of community law are punishable by effective criminal penalties. the court of justice has held that the principle of proportionality is not a principle of community law, but that it is a principle of community law, and that the principle of proportionality is not a principle of community law. the report therefore states that, in order to be legal, such a community initiative in the present legal situation must be exercised only in cases where effective compliance with community provisions can only be ensured in this way. finally, the report proposes that the european commission, as the guardian of the community's interests, should be able to institute or pursue legal proceedings, at least in cases where the member states are entitled to do so. it is encouraging that the constitutional assembly is moving along the same wavelength with the final proposals of the proposed resolution, as shown by articles i-13, iii-65 and iii-172. when the new treaty comes into force we shall have to look at this again.

commission. the commission is aware that the ambient air quality situation, particularly in metropolitan cities such as athens, needs to be improved. this is a major aim of current community legislation on air quality and emissions. in compliance with the reporting obligations of the air quality framework directive, greece has reported the 2001 concentration levels for the pollutants regulated in the first daughter directive. according to this information, the limit values for pm10, as well as for no2, plus the margin of tolerance, have been exceeded at several stations in athens. as greece has not yet provided the necessary justification to demonstrate that such excesses of pm10 are due to natural events, the commission expects to receive plans and programmes in accordance with article 8 of the framework directive by the end of 2003. these should show how greece intends to achieve the limit values by 2005. the same applies to no2 where, however, no derogation for natural sources or events is allowed. for no2 the directives also set an alert threshold which is surpassed when concentrations exceed 400 micrograms per cubic metre over three consecutive hours. the commission must be informed of any exceeding of the alert threshold within three months. no information from the greek authorities on such an event has been provided up to now. the commission has also received findings from a research programme indicating an increase of mortality in cities where high pm10 concentrations are accompanied by high no2 levels and a warm climate. we need to study these findings carefully to conclude whether there is sufficient evidence for such a relationship. however, there is no doubt that unfavourable climatic conditions are always an additional threat to human health. member states are obliged to ensure that up-to-date information on ambient concentration of air pollutants, such as no2 or pm10, is routinely made available to the public. according to the honourable member, the ministry has stopped issuing information on this matter. in the light of the above, the commission will open an own-initiative case to investigate whether and to what extent the greek authorities have not complied with the relevant ec regulations.

in writing. - (el) behind the apparently neutral title 'on the legal bases and respect for community law', the own-initiative report of the legal affairs committee conceals the total subordination of national criminal law to community law. in line with the eu's philosophy, the report argues that the community should be able to oblige member states to impose specific criminal sanctions in the event of a breach of community law. the term 'criminal sanctions' conveys the idea of very heavy penalties, which distinguishes it from administrative or financial sanctions already imposed by eu leaders. the report also proposes that the commission may bring civil proceedings before national criminal courts and even oblige member states to impose prison sentences decided by the community. the only thing left to do is to see the creation of community prisons to enforce community sanctions! this is a further violation of national sovereignty and the so-called "rule of law" of the bourgeoisie, since a supranational body is entrusted with the task of exercising criminal jurisdiction and deciding the type and extent of the penalty. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption by the end of the year.
