commission. - mr president, the commission welcomes the work of mr perry, as evidenced not only by this report but also by the efforts made over the last few months to help reform the directive in the interests of our citizens. on 6 january the commission adopted the fourth report on the application of the directive and a work programme for its review, including a public consultation phase. what have we noted in this implementation report? firstly, the directive is working quite well. however, recent technological developments call for further reflection. the aim of the public consultation was to provide the commission with an assessment of the need to update or amend the directive, and this is where the report and today's discussion will help us. as part of its work programme, the commission organised two series of public hearings in april and june, and interested parties were invited to participate in the public debate by answering specific questions and providing us with their answers. we received 160 written contributions, all of which are available on the commission's website, with the exception of a few contributions for which the authors requested confidentiality. on the basis of the analysis of the results of this consultation, the commission intends to submit a communication to parliament and the council at the end of 2003 or the beginning of 2004 on the future of audiovisual policy, together with possible proposals. one of the challenges of the review is to take technological innovation into account. in this context, i have in mind the 1998 council recommendation on the protection of minors and human dignity in audiovisual and information services, which is the first legal instrument to deal with the content of online audiovisual services broadcast on the internet. the commission intends to publish a second report on the implementation of the recommendation in the coming year, based on a questionnaire sent to the member states. the aim of this report is to report on progress, to allow for direct comparison and to include the new member states as well. mr perry raises a number of questions in his report which i would like to answer, without prejudice, of course, to the consultations which are under way. first, the scope of the directive, points 7 to 12. mr perry advocates the extension of the definition of audiovisual content to take account of the convergence of media. however, as long as broadcasting services have an uneven importance and impact in our societies, it seems difficult to reach a consensus on the concept of content without borders. this is what the consultation showed. and as long as information society services are at an early stage of development, i think it would be inappropriate at this stage of the negotiations to subject them to the more detailed approach of the directive. the very first thing to do is therefore to check whether the directive provides the appropriate regulatory framework for the coming years or whether a change is necessary, which will be done in the communication. as regards the working party of national regulators, point 19, the commission already had a meeting with the regulators last march and the next meeting is scheduled for 14 october. some member states, however, do not see the need for an additional committee and have already expressed fears that this committee will be duplicative. i am not in favour of systematic participation by public and private broadcasters, but rather of invitations on an ad hoc basis as we are doing at the moment. as regards self-regulation and co-regulation - paragraph 20 of the report - i agree with the rapporteur that co-regulation should be allowed to play a more important role. that is why we have specifically raised this question in the working papers and i think we will be able to make progress in this direction. i now come to point 28, with the pan-european channels, and i do not think that the commission is going to take the initiative in this area. moreover, in view of the disappointing results of a study on the possibilities of using digital platforms for thematic channels, it seemed difficult for the commission to finance further studies on this subject. however, we will continue to contribute indirectly to the creation of pan-european channels by establishing a favourable regulatory framework and by supporting the creation and broadcasting of european audiovisual works. as regards the question of television for the disabled - point 34 - it should be noted that the directive deals mainly with content-related aspects and, therefore, the issue of disabled people is not formally addressed in the report on the application of the directive because it does not fall within its scope. it is for the member states to apply the principle of subsidiarity in this area. however, access to television services for disabled people is very important. my services have received several contributions on these relevant issues and all of these contributions are available on the commission's website. you will also find the contributions of associations representing disabled people. in order to make progress in this direction, we intend, together with the royal national institute for the deaf people and the royal national institute for the blind in the united kingdom, to organise a round table on 21 october and invite member states to report on the situation at national level. so we will continue along this line and, by the way, i should also like to tell you that the information society dg has set up a working group called 'inclusive communications'. so this aspect is taken into account. finally, as regards the concentration of the media, which is dealt with in paragraphs 36 to 42, i support the idea of the perry report that pluralism is an important element in safeguarding democracy. this idea is fully reflected in the charter of fundamental rights. i would also like to point out that one of the issues addressed in the green paper on services of general interest of may 2003 relates precisely to the protection of pluralism. all interested parties are invited to submit their comments by 15 september. the commission will determine its future policy on pluralism on the basis of the conclusions of this consultation process. finally, as regards the other amendments to the directive, i will not be able to comment on all of them today because we have not yet received all the written consultations. we receive new ones every day and i would like to allow my staff to complete the analysis of all these contributions before informing you through the communication on audiovisual policy.
the committee on legal affairs and the internal market has adopted an opinion on the proposal. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the legal basis for the directive is established. the rapporteur and i have worked together and i am pleased to say that we are on the same page. the commission must pay particular attention to mr perry's individual proposals in order to i suggest. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i must first of all inform you that my colleague, the minister responsible for this matter, mr lunardi, has unfortunately been detained in rome for important governmental commitments and will therefore not be able to take part in this debate. i shall therefore be brief in making a few comments on this important subject. the council first of all reaffirms its commitment to the development strategy established by the gothenburg european council in 2001. in this respect, our aim is to ensure the sustainability of transport, to address increasing traffic volumes and levels of congestion, noise and pollution, and to promote the use of environmentally friendly modes of transport, as well as the full internationalisation of social and environmental costs. as the european council has stressed, a key instrument for achieving this objective is the development of the trans-european transport networks, with a view to giving priority, where appropriate, to investments in infrastructure for public transport and railways, inland waterways, short sea shipping, intermodal operations and effective interconnection, i.e. the promotion of the development of modes of transport which are less harmful to the environment. the existing guidelines for the development of trans-european transport networks already identify as one of the objectives of the network the ensuring of sustainable mobility of people and goods, while contributing to the achievement of community objectives, in particular in the field of the environment and competition. in this respect, the integration of environmental concerns into project design and development has been set as a priority objective of the development of the network. in general, council directive 85/337/eec of 27 june 1985 requires member states to take account of the protection of the environment by carrying out environmental impact assessments when developing and implementing projects. in addition, an environmental assessment of plans and programmes drawn up in preparation for such projects, in particular those financed by the community, is carried out in accordance with directive 2001/42/ec of 27 june 2001 on the assessment of the effects of certain plans and programmes on the environment. a fully integrated transport network is a prerequisite for the effective free movement of goods and passengers and links islands, peripheral or isolated areas with central regions. a modern, interconnected and interoperable network ensures, through better use of transport, increased trade and the competitiveness of the european economy as a whole. until the necessary infrastructure is in place and a proper regulatory framework for the effective management of the network is in place, the concepts of the internal market and territorial cohesion of the union will remain incomplete. the inclusion in the maastricht treaty of a title devoted to the policy on transeuropean networks has given the european community the necessary powers and instruments for their development. under article 154 of the treaty establishing the european community, the community contributes to the establishment and development of trans-european networks in the fields of transport, telecommunications and energy infrastructure. the above is intended to contribute both to the creation of an internal market and to economic and social cohesion, although this requires first of all the development of the interconnection and interoperability of national networks. the past decade has seen not only a worrying increase in traffic congestion in urban areas, but also a new phenomenon of congestion on the main arteries of the transeuropean network. according to the commission, the external costs of congestion due to road traffic alone represent 0.5% of the eu's gdp. this assessment is all the more alarming if we consider that transport demand will continue to increase substantially in the future. if no measures are taken between now and 2010 to rationalise the use and maximise the benefits of each mode of transport, heavy goods traffic on rubber alone in the eu-15 could increase by 50% compared with 1998. this is a problem not only for the member states but also for the countries applying for accession to the community, as the market share of railways has been gradually declining and road transport has increased by almost 20% between 1990 and 1998. in the new context of sustainable development, the gothenburg european council of june 2001 called for the future emphasis to be placed on the development of rail, maritime and inland waterway transport. ten countries are due to join the european union in may 2004, while romania and bulgaria are expected to join in 2007. these prospects highlight the need for new infrastructure in the corridors serving other countries, with a view to effectively connecting them to the transeuropean network of the current 15 member states. there is also a need to improve links between these countries. a new infrastructure network in the east-west and north-south directions must therefore be created. it should also be recalled that the council conclusions on the second review of the council strategy on the integration of environmental needs and sustainable development into transport policy, adopted by transport ministers in december 2002, stressed the importance of analysing new policy proposals from the point of view of the environmental impact and the community's ability to reduce the harmful impacts on the environment of the transport sector. in support of this approach, i would remind you that at the same meeting last december the council approved the marco polo programme, which is intended to finance the improvement of the environmental performance of the freight transport system. the programme provides for the financing of initiatives to transfer freight transport from road to other modes such as rail, inland waterway and maritime cabotage. the objective of promoting sustainable development through efforts to rebalance modes of transport in favour of environmentally friendly modes of transport will therefore be a key criterion for the council when, in the coming months, it examines the commission proposal for the revision of the ten guidelines and the priority projects contained therein. in this context, the council considers that the conclusions of the high level group, chaired by former commissioner van miert, are in line with the strategic guidelines for sustainable and balanced development, which is concerned with protecting the environment and at the same time desires to promote the unity of europe through the free movement of people and goods, the reduction of natural barriers, the balance of the east-west and north-south axes, and considers that infrastructure investment, suitably accompanied by public-private partnership initiatives, can be a formidable tool for supporting economic growth. the case of some countries is emblematic in this respect, for which the problem of crossings remains and continues to cause considerable economic damage to the country's production system. that is why we must continue to call on the commission to solve these problems. the council therefore urges the commission to present its proposal for the revision of the tens as soon as possible, so that a common position can be adopted after a broad political debate.

the rapporteur. - (it) mr president, i have asked for my speech to be divided into two parts: the first now, which will be three minutes long, and the second, which will be two minutes long, at the end of the debate. i now want to talk about the interinstitutional agreement on better lawmaking. this agreement is the result of long and difficult negotiations during which we all asked ourselves - parliament, the commission and the council, but above all we ourselves, i must say - whether it would not be better to give up quietly, given the difficulty of finding real advantages in the current situation. first of all, i would like to thank mr gargani, mr swoboda and mr clegg, with whom we have had a good working relationship, and the technical group that negotiated with us, because in any case we have finally reached a positive result. so if we are here to encourage parliament to vote in favour of this agreement, it is because i think that progress - albeit minor and tentative - has been made. i would like to focus in particular on two issues which i believe are particularly important: co-regulation and self-regulation. not because the results we have achieved are revolutionary, but because i believe that if we use it properly - particularly in this house - this agreement will make it easier for us to combat a very worrying trend which the commission and the council, i am sorry to say, seem to be embracing. it is the tendency to move towards alternative methods of regulation to legislation and i am referring here specifically to what we call voluntary agreements. recent experience in the field of road safety and co2 emissions from cars has shown us that the risks of not achieving the objectives that can be achieved by normal legislation in terms of efficiency and systematic application are very real when these voluntary agreements are used. it is precisely to respond to this potential danger that we have been very much involved in this difficult debate, which also included many other elements - as members will see if they read the text, there is also a lot of filler - but at least some minor progress has been made on the issues of self-regulation and co-regulation. however, we must admit that we have failed in one area: we have not been able to obtain the right of call back from the commission - the right to suspend the use of a voluntary agreement if we do not approve it. we are extremely disappointed because it was the commission - and i must say this - that did not want to be disturbed. we have simply obtained a political will on the part of the commission to take account of the clear and unequivocal opposition of parliament. if it is deemed necessary, it will then be for parliament to organise its opposition to the voluntary agreement in order to force the commission to recall it itself. one last thing, mr president: the difficulty facing the commission and the council in making progress in this area is exactly the same as that which we faced in the negotiations on comitology. we hope that it has been overcome once and for all by the agreements reached by the convention.

in writing. - (el) even if we admit that the objectives of a reduction in the fishing fleet have not been achieved - which is not the case in greece, for example, where we have even recorded a reduction in the fleet and fisheries to the benefit of imports and aquaculture - we have no reason to deplore the failure of the multiannual guidance programmes. the reason is that these programmes mark the beginning of restrictions on the production of small and medium-sized fisheries undertakings, as is the case in greece, leading to a decline in fishing, a deterioration in the sector's trade balance and adverse consequences for the populations of coastal regions. we agree with the control of the fishing capacity of the fleet, but we do not agree with the control of the fishing capacity by the common fisheries policy, as stipulated in the multiannual guidance programmes. on the contrary, we believe that the responsibility for regulation should lie with the member states, which should take compliance measures based on real scientific data provided by other bodies, such as fao, on the state of fish stocks, etc. in no case can we accept the attribution of this responsibility to supranational bodies such as the eu, because its policy contributes to the strengthening of large enterprises, also in the fisheries sector, while at the same time attacking small and medium-sized fisheries by withdrawing and tearing up boats, by measures to support aquaculture, etc.

the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank you for the opportunity to report on the achievements of the european year of disabled people and the follow-up to it, given that we are a month and a half away from the end of the year. we must bear in mind that disability policies are national policies and the effort made in 2003 is to find all those methods, tools and channels by which we can add european added value to national policies. to date, the year has achieved important objectives related to raising awareness of the rights of persons with disabilities. we have thousands of events in all the member states at national, regional and local level, discussions in parliaments and forums, exchange of good practices between member states, and of course ngos and the disabled people's movement have really contributed to an explosion of events and dissemination of the message about the rights of people with disabilities. the european parliament has given its full support to the year from the outset. on 3 november 2003, the first hearing on lifelong learning opportunities for young people with disabilities was held in parliament, and a few days ago, on 10 and 11 november, the european parliament of people with disabilities met and adopted a resolution to this effect. it is, of course, important to stress that the year is the beginning of a european process and that all the effort and planning does not end at the end of the year. it is extremely important to use the potential that has been developed and it must be said that today in all countries initiatives and innovative actions have been taken, which did not exist in the past, and we also have important legislation, which has been highly promoted in some countries. on 30 october the commission adopted a communication on the follow-up to the year. the main objectives are three. the first is to achieve the adoption and full implementation of the directive on equal treatment in employment and work for people with disabilities. the second is the successful integration of disability issues into all policies. this is our agreement on mainstreaming, so that this policy is not a matter for the ministries of social affairs or the ministries of health or the ministries of employment, but is a horizontal policy that involves all ministries in each country and all portfolios in the commission. the third is to improve accessibility for all. as regards the first point, the implementation of the directive, ladies and gentlemen, i would remind you that in 2000 an anti-discrimination directive was adopted in record time, unprecedented in the european union, but it must be said that the member states did not promote it as quickly as we had hoped. the commission has already proposed a number of amendments to the directive on equal treatment for people who are discriminated against. the deadline expires at the end of december and only two countries have effectively adopted the directive. but beyond adoption, we will have to move on to implementation, where we will need to make major changes to the rules currently in force in some member states. this will have an impact on employers, both in the public and private sectors, and on the employment practices applied to disabled people, because the letter of the directive on reasonable accommodation will have to be applied. in other words, the workplace should be adapted to the needs of disabled people. the commission will do its duty as guardian of the treaty, and will do its duty to ensure that the directive is adopted at the right time, that it is transposed correctly - not in the wrong way, not without the specific references in the european text - and, of course, that it is implemented. the communication, as i said, has also focused on the issue of horizontal policies concerning disabled people and integration into all individual policies, and we already have examples at european level, with an important step in the field of transport and in the field of electronic communications, the responsibilities of commissioners de palacio and liikanen. the mainstreaming of these issues into all relevant policies should focus on access issues, access to goods, services, buildings, and should be linked to the principle of 'design for all' as set out in the commission's immediately preceding communication. the communication sets out a multiannual rolling action plan. the first priority is employment, which is also the most important factor in the social integration of people with disabilities. i would say that our philosophy is essentially that disabled people should have the right to work and not to receive benefits. the first stage of the action plan, to be developed in 2004 and 2005, will therefore focus on creating the necessary conditions for promoting the employment of people with disabilities. we now estimate that there are 3 million disabled people in europe who could be integrated into the labour market. there are even more people who, with specific policies, with investment in these people and with qualifications commensurate with their capabilities, could enter the labour market. our employment policy will focus on four priorities: access to and retention in employment, lifelong learning, new technologies - which we believe to be one of the most critical elements - because through innovation and research a range of new skills can, across all types of disabilities, really empower these people to deal with their individual disabilities. but at the same time, these tools should be cheap and accessible to everyone. the european market is extremely difficult for these people today. each country has its own specifications, each social system is linked to its own enterprises, so that the same tools are cheap in one country and expensive in another. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a good example of the need to ensure that the directive is applied in all member states. as a means of supporting the successful integration of these issues into policies, the commission proposed the publication of a biannual report announcing the developments made in each member state and covering the focus each time on planning and new priority options. we believe that this report - the first of which will be published in 2005 - will be an important instrument for putting pressure on the member states, which should announce and publish every two years the developments at institutional and implementation level. finally, the commission proposes to further enhance the involvement of all stakeholders and key actors in policy dialogue so that we can have large but also lasting changes in the whole of the economy and society. i would like to express my satisfaction at the opportunity given to carry out a study, as requested by parliament, on the situation of people with disabilities living in institutions, who are another large category of our fellow citizens with particular and other problems. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. mr president, expectations for the year were high. i think we have significant results, especially if we consider - as i pointed out in my introduction - that these policies are largely, almost entirely, national policies. but i believe that all this activation of the year in 2003 has brought the issue of people with disabilities to the top of the political agenda of both the member states and the european union itself. but above all, it brought the disabled people's movement itself to the forefront of politics, putting into practice the slogan "nothing for us without us", that is, their necessary participation at all levels of planning and decision-making.

- the report (α5-0385/2003) by mrs miguélez ramos, on behalf of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the improvement of the safety of ships and port facilities is on the agenda.
the commission's vice-president - (es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the recent wave of attacks has also affected the european union. this morning we observed a minute's silence in memory of the young italian soldiers, but also of the iraqi civilians who lost their lives. it is clear that no country or sector is immune. whether we like it or not, such acts can happen anywhere and at any time, for any reason. the maritime sector is no exception. i would remind you of the case of the cruise ship achille lauro. it is true that this was in 1985, but since then the limburg oil tanker has also been the target of a terrorist attack. the commission proposal aims to promote the effective and harmonised implementation of the security measures for ships and port facilities ratified by the member states of the union in the framework of the international maritime organisation. the proposal aims to create a common maritime security area guaranteeing an identical level of security for all maritime trade within the european union. this proposal is in line with the text adopted by parliament and the council on civil aviation safety. in both the maritime and civil aviation sectors, a determined action by the european union in the field of security can only prove to our international partners that we take all security-related issues very seriously. instruments adopted within the framework of the international maritime organisation shall apply only to ships engaged in international trade and to port facilities hosting such ships. it would be desirable to extend certain provisions of these instruments to national maritime traffic within europe in order to achieve the overall objective of safety in the maritime transport sector. it is therefore essential to ensure that the measures to be applied are proportionate to the risks involved. priority must be given to passenger transport. the proposal goes further than some of the provisions adopted by the international maritime organisation. it thus makes the application of certain provisions which were considered only as recommendations in the who agreement mandatory, in order to guarantee the maximum level of safety provided for and to prevent divergent interpretations by member states. to that end, it shall establish a single national contact point responsible for the supervision of security measures for ships and port facilities. the proposal also contains a provision for a commission supervised inspection procedure to ensure the implementation of the national plans adopted under this regulation. the proposal also adapts certain provisions adopted under the imo to the national maritime traffic of the member states. it extends the scope of the who safety measures for passenger ships sailing on inland waterways more than 20 nautical miles from the coast. the application of this measure is extended to all other passenger ships operating on domestic routes. cargo ships will also be affected to some extent. in addition, there is a provision for adaptation procedures for ships on regular services. i would like to reiterate once again that the imo is determined to bring these maritime safety measures into force as from 1 july 2004. the main objective of this proposal for a regulation is to ensure that the member states of the union adopt the necessary measures within the time limit. it will ensure that member states respect their international commitments and that the application of these measures is harmonised throughout the european union. it's imperative that everything is in place by the deadline. i can therefore only support any action leading to rapid adoption without prejudice to the content. i note that parliament and the rapporteur are fully aware of this. they have been working with the council for several months now to get the text adopted as quickly as possible, preferably at first reading. in this connection, i would like to thank mrs miguélez ramos for her excellent work. i also thank the whole of parliament for its efforts to reach a quick, flexible and effective solution in the interests of the citizens of the european union.
the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy has adopted a number of amendments to the proposal. mr president, i would like to congratulate the committee and the rapporteur because the need for the development of safe ports and shipping is proving to be very great every day. and i understand the urgency of this matter. i have to complain, however, that a proposal by the committee on industry to co-finance the cost of these measures was rejected. a study carried out by the oecd in july 2003 estimates the initial cost of the measures to be taken at $ 1 279 million 'initial investment' and then $ 730 million per year for their maintenance. as you can see, the enormous costs that will be shared by european ports will now have to be borne by the ports, the shipping companies and the small and mediumsized enterprises operating on the periphery of these actions, since there will be no co-financing as proposed by the committee on industry. we are aware that the competitiveness of the european economy will be disproportionately affected in relation to other competitive economies. the fact that jobs are certain to be lost and that small and mediumsized enterprises will be closed has also been ignored. i am afraid that all this has not been taken into account as much as it should have been, and i am afraid that by forcing the regulation to be passed quickly we have sacrificed it.

- the agenda calls for the report (α5-0364/2003) by mr jarzembowski on the joint draft directive of the european parliament and of the council on access to the market for port services, approved by the conciliation committee.
the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, madam vice-president, after tough negotiations, parliament's delegation has succeeded in convincing the council to accept a large number of provisions which are not only favourable to existing port systems and port workers but will also ensure fair conditions of competition in and between ports. although we have not been able to persuade the council to accept certain requirements, i would recommend that all members of this house accept the result of the conciliation procedure and express their satisfaction with it. considerations relating to the legal security of ports, port operators and workers require the european union to adopt a first fundamental directive on ports. rejecting this compromise would mean leaving open for several years more vital issues for european transport policy, in particular market access within ports and the conditions of competition between them, which would open the door to distortions of competition between ports and uncontrollable duplication of their services. let me warn those members of this house who advocate the rejection of the compromise: if it is rejected, the commission would be empowered to examine the situation in each port. it would be better to set up basic rules so that everyone knows from the outset which rules to follow. parliament is particularly pleased that the council has accepted its request that the definition of self-help should cover only seafarers in shipping companies and not personnel on shore. in this connection, parliament was able to express in concrete terms the main concerns of port operators and workers. in order to reach this compromise, the parliament delegation also had to abandon its general requirement for prior authorisation for port services. the council intends to apply the principle of subsidiarity and leave this competence to the member states. however, we were able to accept the idea that member states should ensure that the competent authorities can require prior authorisation for the provision of port services, so that this is left to the discretion of the member states. the council finally accepted parliament's amendments concerning the time limits and conditions for authorizations and transitional provisions; parliament has thus ensured that equity participation is treated in the same way as leasing contracts. the parliament's delegation also succeeded in imposing the amendment or withdrawal of authorisations in the event of non-compliance with the criteria governing authorisation or the provisions of social legislation. it is therefore important to stress that we have taken an unambiguous position on the social conditions of dock workers and have done a remarkable job. the council has also accepted that member states should adopt provisions requiring new service providers to pay appropriate compensation to previous providers, but - and we are not satisfied with this request - the council wishes to limit this provision to providers whose authorization period is reduced by the new directive. some see a certain logic in this request. national legislation must apply in all other cases. parliament has had to accept with regret that piloting services remain within the scope of the directive. this requirement is however considered acceptable, given the particular importance that the council and the parliament attach to piloting services for safety and environmental protection and the fact that the competent authorities may limit piloting activity to a single provider for reasons of public safety. parliament finally succeeded in removing the council's limitation on the duration of the licence for piloting services. i think that parliament has taken a further step and succeeded in extending the objectives of the directive to include the establishment of fair conditions of competition in and between ports. to this end, ports and providers of port services shall disclose to the member states and the commission the financial relationships they have with public authorities. the commission, for its part, has an obligation to take the necessary measures to eliminate distortions of competition and has already stated its willingness to adopt explicit guidelines on the amount of public subsidies allowed in ports. in conclusion, i would like to stress that the outcome of the conciliation procedure is a great success for all of us, given the extremely negative attitude which the council initially showed. i would like to thank in particular the italian presidency of the council and the vice-president for having enabled us to bring this complex matter to a successful conclusion. let me make one last remark: we are not dealing with isolated problems specific to ports. the ability of eu ports to compete is also at stake, given their crucial role as nodes in the trans-european networks. we all have a responsibility to improve the efficiency of these ports, and i therefore ask you to accept and support the outcome of the conciliation procedure.
vice-president of the commission. (es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank the house and the conciliation committee for their work on the proposal for a directive on market access for port services. i would like to thank in particular the chairman of the conciliation committee, mr imbeni, and the rapporteur, mr jarzembowski, for the hard work they have put into such a complex matter. the house is called to vote on a compromise approved by the conciliation committee. i want to make it very clear that the commission supports this compromise; although i know that there are some members who are opposed to it, i would ask members to think carefully before rejecting this compromise. i consider this an essential commitment for european transport policy. this commitment does not, in any way, suggest the liberalisation of port services, as i have heard during the previous debate. not by a long shot. it is only a small opening for certain types of services to be provided by self-handling, that is, by the on-board staff only. ladies and gentlemen, we are talking every day about wanting environmentally friendly and sustainable transport, about wanting to import short sea shipping, short sea shipping, so we cannot vote the next day against a measure which is going to facilitate the development of this type of transport. what i want to say to the honourable members is that we have to be consistent in our approaches. the proposal we are voting on, especially as it has come out of the discussions in parliament, the amendments by parliament, the negotiations with the council, is a very balanced proposal, very moderate, but one which can clearly serve to boost maritime cabotage, an essential issue in ensuring a sustainable transport system in europe. it has been three years of negotiations and i simply think that to reject this initiative would pose very serious problems for transport policy in the years to come. i would like to remind you of some aspects of the text which will be put to the vote on thursday. the original proposal was limited to rules applicable within a given port. parliament insisted strongly on the need to address the question of competition between ports and this point, which the commission took up, has been corrected in the final text with the council's agreement. the commission's initial proposal concerned self-help with on-board and ground staff. it is true, we were opening up the question of self-help for companies with ground staff. parliament raised two kinds of questions: one, social guarantees to prevent social dumping, which the commission accepted, and two, to limit even further the scope of self-help and to restrict it to the staff on board. right now, we're talking only about the personnel on board. it is obvious that this self-help of the on-board staff will work with short-distance transport. it will not work with large trans-oceanic transports because of the type of goods being transported and the type of ship being used. so we are talking about something that is key to the development of short-distance transport. parliament's position has therefore been maintained and self-help has been limited to on-board staff. and, in addition, with some of the social rules to which i referred earlier. in the initial proposal, placement was considered a commercial service subject to all the rules. parliament raised the question of excluding apprenticeships and in the end we reached an agreement which is somewhat open in terms of apprenticeships. but let us be very clear: the apprenticeship service is not being liberalized. what we are talking about is that, for example - and once again we are talking about cabotage and short sea shipping - a captain who makes a route every day, or two or three times a week, who knows the route perfectly well, can eventually get a licence so as not to need the practice. we are talking about a measure which is key for short sea shipping. this will not affect trans-oceanic traffic where the ship arrives at the same port once, twice or five times a year. this question concerns only those ships which have regular lines, that is to say, once again the question of short sea shipping, of maritime cabotage. i would like to say, ladies and gentlemen, that the commission has been extremely flexible throughout this whole discussion. because we believe that some of the measures proposed by the honourable members have improved the texts - i have not referred to them, because they were not controversial. we have tried to balance as much as possible the problems raised or reflected by others, including those of a political nature. what remains at the end is the minimum, but it is a vital minimum, and i want to emphasize this point, vital to be able to promote cabotage, especially cabotage within the european union. i would therefore ask you to support, to vote in favour of, this compromise proposal which was reached the other day in the conciliation committee. i would like to thank once again mr imbeni and, of course, mr jarzembowski for their work over the years.
mr president, today with the jarzembowski report, which i congratulate on the long effort it has taken to get here, we are essentially doing nothing more than what we did when parliament asked for the postal services to be opened up to competition, the rail services to competition, the air transport to competition. it would be strange if this parliament, which played a leading role in opening up these services, were to come and say that for reasons that are incomprehensible to me at least, there must be an exception to this long series of opening up the market for all these services, and that exception must be port services. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's fishing fleet is not disrupted by the introduction of a new system of fishing quotas, which is not yet in place. so, to me at least, it is frankly incomprehensible why some people are still opposed to what we have achieved and which, we must know, does not make the industry entirely happy, particularly the shipowners, who would like something more daring. i, for my part, think that this compromise before us serves to some extent the interests of industry, since there are other providers, it breaks the monopoly and there is more choice, but it also serves the workers because in this way new businesses are created and new businesses mean new jobs. it is therefore a step forward, mr president, and that is why we must support the outcome of the conciliation and vote in favour.

in writing. the general electronic identification of sheep and goats is a modern system which will essentially be the indelible identity of each small animal, which is essential to identify it wherever it is and to monitor its health without any doubt. however, without community funding, such labelling imposes a heavy financial burden on sheep and goat farmers. in greece in particular, where sheep and goat farming employs the whole family of the farmer, day and night, 365 days a year, without christmas and easter and with an unacceptably low economic output in relation to the effort paid and the capital invested, such an unreasonable and unfair financial burden would lead many producers to abandon their work and the countryside and the livestock stock to a tragic decline. consequently, cheese factories producing only goat and sheep milk would close, adding unemployed artisanal cheese-makers and cheese-makers to the ranks of unemployed farmers, while reducing the production of the only greek cheeses based on goat and sheep milk, such as feta. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval. at the same time, however, the general introduction of electronic identification of sheep and goats by 1 july 2006 is considered too hasty for greece, where the number of sheep and goats is greater than the total of sheep and goats in the other 14 member states. that period should therefore be extended by at least one year.

commission. mr president, since this is a joint debate, the bad news is that i shall have to speak at some length, but the good news is i will be as quick as i possibly can whilst not avoiding responding to the detailed issues that have been raised by honourable members in their activities, which i know reflect the hard and intensive work they have been doing. as this house knows, the three european institutions worked together to secure a new financial regulation in 2002 that will come into effect on 1 january 2003. the regulation provides inter alia a clear framework for subsidies through which we support a large number of european organisations in the dialogue with european citizens, and it also stipulates that each financial decision should have a legal basis to ensure its justification. that requirement is particularly relevant for those subsidies which have been financed from lines whose position in the budgetary structure the so-called a-part of the budget meant that they could be assimilated into administrative expenditure and consequently be incurred without a clear legal basis. the modification of the budgetary structure introduced in the new financial regulation has brought to an end this assimilation of administrative expenditure, meaning that a legal basis for the subsidies in question is now required. it is this new obligation which led the commission in may 2003 to present seven proposals for new legal bases. these were accompanied by a communication from mrs schreyer, which underlined the common context and presented identical solutions for common problems. the commission welcomes this report by mr sacrédeus and appreciates the priority which the drafters and parliament have given to dealing with the commission’s proposal. with parliament’s opinion it should now be possible to have the decision in force in 2004 and following a call for proposals, to go ahead with the selection of beneficiaries for operating grants for next year. the goal agreed between parliament and council during the conciliation of 16 july was the entry into force, by 2004, of the legal bases for grants which did not have that coverage. the legal base presented today, together with the six other proposals covering grants, is important because it is a direct consequence of the innovations concerning grants in the new financial regulation and is firmly anchored in the basic principles of transparency and equal treatment for potential beneficiaries. most of the amendments proposed in parliament's resolution are acceptable to the commission and in keeping with the spirit of the commission’s proposal. however, the commission thinks it appropriate to limit the amount of the grant to 70% of the eligible costs and not 80%. similarly, the commission is of the view that a digressivity rate of 10% per year is preferable to 2.5%. our view is that both of these requirements are safeguards which will go some way to ensuring sustainability and encouraging beneficiaries to be active in seeking alternative and complementary revenue streams. one point which should be mentioned is the need to ensure coherence between the proposed council decision and the budget. in the preliminary draft budget the commission proposed one budget line to regroup amounts which, in the 2003 budget, are distributed over four lines in chapter a 30. the future legal base for this single line, as required by the new financial regulation, is the proposed decision which is before the house today. this decision provides for the selection of beneficiaries following a call for proposals in accordance with the principles of transparency and equal treatment. at first reading, parliament replaced the single line with five lines. the title of each line is the name of an institute. there is a clear incompatibility between the future legal base and the division of the budget line in this manner. the commission hopes that the adopted budget will correspond to the pdb proposal, so permitting us to execute the proposal and appropriations in full compliance with european law as defined by the new financial regulation adopted by this house and the council. i now turn to the report by mrs rühle on the proposal for an action programme to promote civic participation. i am grateful to mrs rühle for having acknowledged the urgency of this matter and for having ensured speedy adoption by the committee on citizens' freedoms and rights, justice and home affairs. this has been immensely helpful. the commission's proposal before the house seeks to ensure harmonious transition from the old system to the new arrangements and continuity in the activities being supported. we have endeavoured to produce a text which, to a large extent, extends the 2003 implementation procedures while incorporating the requirements of the new financial regulation in terms of sound financial management of public funds. this proposal for a legal basis should therefore be considered a technical adjustment. there is, nevertheless, a great and understandable temptation to grasp the opportunity to add innovations and suggest improvements. parliament, as ever, is immensely helpful with this creativity. this may, however, be risky particularly if such additions compromise the subsequent adoption of the proposal by the council. the commission's proposal has therefore been formulated in what we consider to be a measured way, with the essential objective of continuing what has already been accomplished and by providing a legal structure which is consistent with the new financial regulation. i would consequently invite honourable members not to distance themselves too much from the commission's proposals and to do their utmost to ensure that this legal basis is adopted as quickly as possible. furthermore, in the case of the legal basis for active civic participation, the margin for manoeuvre is even more limited because unanimity is required in council. all avenues for compromise must be explored if we are to succeed in completing this procedure as speedily as possible. in fact, as from 1 january 2004, in the absence of this legal basis, it would quite simply not be possible for us to provide financial support to all the organisations which participate actively in the promotion of european citizenship. we would greatly regret that, and doubtless parliament would too. i shall now outline the position of the commission on the amendments contained in mrs rühle's report. the commission can accept in full amendments 1, 4, 7, 9, 11, 12, 15, 16, 13 and 31, which provide useful clarifications to the text. while recalling the need to apply the new financial regulation, the commission sees no objection to amendment 45 on the simplification of administrative procedures. it goes without saying that the commission will impose an obligation on those who have received a european subsidy to provide adequate publicity. while entirely agreeing with parliament on this point, as outlined in amendment 48, we feel that it would be more appropriate to list this obligation in the conventions to be signed with the beneficiaries. the same holds true for amendment 49 on the dissemination and availability of results. the commission agrees with amendment 47, which underlines the need for regular exchanges of views with the beneficiaries. the commission can partly accept amendment 25. since the amendment does not alter the substance of the commission proposal, we can accept the proposal to specify that the budgetary appropriations scheduled after 2006 are subject to an agreement of the budgetary authority on the financial perspective beyond 2006. however, the commission is willing to accept the same duration for all seven proposals in the package until 2006 if that helps to find a compromise for all the proposals with a view to having them adopted in time for implementing the budget in 2004. as this proposal has to be seen in conjunction with the other proposals in the package, the amendments on 'earmarking' and the possibility of an executive agency also have to be settled in the broader context. the commission cannot accept, in the same amendment, a reference to the total amount allocated to the programme since this is not consistent with the legislative procedures provided for in the consultation procedure. the commission can also partially accept amendment 28. we have no objections to sending reports on implementation of the programme, but we cannot accept transferring the content of the annex to article 8a, which would not be in line with the usual format of legal texts. the same applies to amendments 20, 21, 22, 29 and 30, which the commission rejects. the commission understands the view of parliament on the matter of focusing on potential enlargement of the scope and objectives of this proposal. however, it is our intention to guarantee the continuity of the activities already supported by the commission in the past, so we have to refuse amendments 14, 40, 41, 42 and 43, with a view to reaching a unanimous position on our proposal in the council. amendments 6 and 33, concerning the european movement, are rejected as well as amendments 32, 34, 35, 36 and 37, which add new organisations to the list of beneficiaries. with a view to ensuring the regulation, we intend to launch a call for proposals which will be open to all organisations active in this area. however, to facilitate the transition from the system of 'earmarking' to the system of calls for proposals, and taking into account the time left before the programme enters into force, we consider it more appropriate to apply the model of earmarking for 2004, and to publish an open call for proposals as from 2005. this would be a reasonable compromise since it would be technically impossible, under the procedures laid down in the financial regulation, to launch a call for proposals after the adoption of this legal base which would still allow for financing as from the beginning of 2004. as a consequence, the commission can, in principal, accept the application of a system of 'earmarking'. we consider, however, that this approach should be restricted to 2004 and the operating rules should be laid down in the annex rather than in the text of the programme. usual format of legal texts and is also rejected. on the possible involvement of an executive agency for the management of part of the programme, particularly in relation to management of the large number of projects in the town-twinning part of the programme, the commission emphasises that such an approach conforms to article 55 of the financial regulation applicable to the general budget of currently under preparation by an external consultant, the commission could propose that such an agency should be partly involved in the management of this programme. before reaching a final decision, the commission will submit this proposal to the executive agency committee of the council. the commission is therefore not in a position at this juncture to accept amendment 46. the commission rejects in writing. - the day after the igc meeting in naples, there was a marked increase in pressure from the european institutions to impose the convention's constitutional project, and thus a central and supranational power to manage the enlarged europe. in our opinion, the correct solution would be the opposite: to accept the idea of a differentiated europe, to respect national sovereignty more and to organize the variable geometry clearly. in other words, countries such as spain and poland, which are now accused of delaying the progress of the igc under the convention, by defending their national interests, are in fact defending the general interest of europe, which is to keep nations free and national democracies alive. on the two main points of discussion which will be discussed again at the next brussels council - the composition of the commission and the qualified majority in the council - we recall our proposal of old: the main thing is to recognize a national right of popular opposition, which each people could exercise in solemn forms against a european decision. this innovation, which would rehabilitate national democracies and help to close the democratic deficit, would at the same time make all discussions about the commission and the council relative.
the council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, thank you for inviting me to discuss the economic stability and growth pact with you during this sitting. let me begin by recounting the events leading up to the eurogroup and ecofin meeting on 24 and 25 november. in the first half of 2003, on a proposal from the commission, the council sent two recommendations on excessive deficits to germany and france, on 21 january and 3 june respectively, calling for these deficits to be brought below the 3% reference value by the end of 2004. it should be noted that these recommendations were adopted on the basis of a gradual economic growth assumed during the year following the disappearance of the negative factors due to the end of the war in iraq. however, in the months that followed it became clear that the real growth of the european economy was different, i.e. more negative than expected. economic growth, which was about one percentage point below expectations, led to a larger than expected increase in government deficits. as a result, germany and france were unable to bring their deficits below the 3% mark in 2004 as originally required. in the second half of 2003, between october and november, the commission fully and formally recognised this new situation and therefore proposed two new recommendations to postpone the reduction of the deficit below 3% to 2005. in essence, it is reasonable to assume that if it had been known from the beginning of 2003 that the euro area economy would not grow positively, the recommendations would have set 2005 as the deadline for the alignment of deficits with the norm from the outset. on this basis, germany and france have both adopted measures to incorporate the substance of the recommendations. in germany, the recommendations were incorporated directly into budgetary legislation: a structural adjustment of 0.6% of gdp was planned for 2004 and a 0.5% adjustment was planned for 2005, which amounts to 1.1% of gdp in total, close to the percentage originally required by the commission, without prejudice to the reduction below 3% in 2005. in france, the recommendations were first incorporated into budget legislation and then through other measures: an adjustment of 0.8% of gdp was planned for 2004 and an adjustment of 0.6% was planned for 2005, which amounts to 1.4% of gdp in total, close to the percentage required by the commission, without prejudice to the reduction below 3% in 2005. in addition, france and germany committed themselves to using the possible effects of higher growth to reduce their deficits, as requested by the commission. in addition, it should be borne in mind that in 2003, france and germany launched a major social security reform programme which had a decisive positive impact on the sustainability of public finances. in the context of political economy, this is a major issue surrounding the discussion on the pact which took place during the year. in the main, first in the framework of the work carried out in october and november, then in the eurogroup and finally in ecofin, a broad consensus was reached on the substance of the recommendations made by the commission and on the substance of the adjustments introduced by france and germany. now we come to the procedural questions. the commission proposed the two recommendations in accordance with article 104 (9) on the basis that germany and france continued to fail to act on the council's recommendations. germany and france, while accepting the substance of the recommendations, requested that they be given a different form for political reasons, namely the reformulation of a second set of recommendations in accordance with article 104 (7). the council's legal service, consulted on the matter, said that the commission could also have taken - and i stress the word 'also' - this second route. the commission has excluded this possibility. at this point, the situation was deadlocked: the essential, i.e. the substance, was in danger of being lost for formal reasons. in order to break the deadlock without exacerbating the situation, the eurogroup, on the basis of a broad consensus, incorporated the substance of the recommendations into a draft conclusions. the validity of this procedure has been confirmed once again by the council's legal service. secondly, when ecofin started its work, the commission explicitly expressed its disagreement, requesting a formal vote on the second set of recommendations for germany and france. the required majority was not obtained. it should be stressed that the ecofin council's vote on the commission's recommendations is expressly provided for in the rules currently in force and is therefore fully compatible with them. following the rejection of the commission's recommendations, the council took a position on the conclusions drawn up earlier in the eurogroup. these conclusions were approved and the discussion led to the adoption of the council declaration unanimously. the content of this declaration can be summed up as follows: stability and growth are the fundamental objectives of european economic policy. the pact is an essential means of implementing this policy. the pact was called "stupid". we have proved the contrary, we have shown that the pact can be interpreted in a flexible and discerning way. the pact can be implemented by adjusting budgetary discipline even more rationally to positive or negative economic cycles and by encouraging structural reforms to develop growth potential. in these circumstances, the letter and the spirit of the covenant have not died; on the contrary, we have worked, we are working and we will continue to work within the framework of the pact and with the support of the commission in a cooperative and consensual manner. in conclusion, we have so far spoken a lot about procedure, but hardly about economics. in the growth strategy, as has been said, it is necessary that the pact takes account of economic cycles and structural reforms: this is necessary, but it is not enough. six months ago, at the beginning of this presidency, we presented an action plan for growth to this house. parliament's support for this plan has been decisive. the plan must now be implemented. new development initiatives must follow. the commission, governments and markets have a role to play in the growth strategy, but so does the european parliament, which must provide the necessary impetus: economic policy is policy or it is not.
mr president, most of what i had in mind has already been said and i would like to endorse the speech of mr poettering, who has unfortunately left. i would like to focus our attention on this: the rules that we freely accept and sign, big and small, strong and weak, must be respected by all, whether we like it or not. the european union's principles and regulations are considered to be applied à la carte, and if they are in our interest we respect them, if they displease us we ignore them. the most fundamental principle of democracy is respect for the law by all. if they don't satisfy us, we change them. if it does not satisfy the stability pact, it should be abolished or amended. but in no case can it be considered as valid but not observed by those who do not like it, as has happened now. when the terms of the pact were breached by small eu member states such as portugal, they were forced to implement tough measures and spending cuts to bring their deficit below 3%, and none of the major current breachers asked for the pact not to be applied. now that the problem has hit their economy unexpectedly, they have discovered that the pact is unsuitable to the point of unacceptability. two meters and two scales. the reaction of the small countries is therefore understandable, seeing that 'some are more equal than others', as george orwell said. the european parliament has already expressed its concern about the situation in the former yugoslavia, and has called for the immediate release of all political prisoners.
madam president, 'sticks and carrots' quoth mr watson: there were plenty of sticks and carrots in the stability pact - sticks for the workers and carrots for the managers, sticks for the unemployed and carrots for the financiers. not only was the stability pact socially unfair, it was totally unworkable, and the tragedy about breaking it is not that we did not wish it to be respected, it is that it was ever set up. that was the real tragedy. if we had stuck to the maastricht criteria with the same severity that the stability pact asks us to stick to the three per cent, would there be a euro today? would there be a euro, commissioner? i ask everybody here to put their hand on their heart and answer that question honestly, like honest people who want rules to be respected. the second point about this is that the commission tells us that it will continue applying the pact. if the same case happens again, how will the pact be applied? i hope with the same latitude that was shown to france and germany. it would be unfair for a different standard to be applied to a small country in the future. it has also been suggested that the deficits of today are the taxes of tomorrow. how very simple! the deficits of today can also be the investment of today, which will produce the higher income of tomorrow, from which higher taxes can easily be paid. so i suggest we stop making virtuous speeches here and go and enrol in a good course of elementary macroeconomics, which some of us here seem to need - of course, i am not including the minister in this comment. he seems to know about it - or has learned about it - and i am grateful to him for that. the substance of the matter is that today we need expansionary, rather than contractionary, economic policy. just as there is inflationary stability, there can also be deflationary stability. from that point of view the demise of the stability pact is good for stability.
madam president, the proposed arrangements for the insurance card may remove some bureaucratic procedures, but in practice all their advantages are cancelled out by the policy of reducing social expenditure and benefits in accordance with the maastricht criteria, under the pretext of excessive budget deficits, and by the policy of commercialising health systems. these adjustments will help to speed up the implementation of the european union's policy of capitalist restructuring in the member states, under the pretext of harmonizing health systems, i.e. the downward equalization of social benefits, the abolition of the public sector and the privatization and commercialisation of health and social security systems, the reduction of pensions, the increase in workers' contributions to insurance funds. all of this is a raid on the workers. what good is the card when access to the public health system is becoming increasingly problematic and the privilege of the right to care is left to those who can afford to pay, since even public hospitals operate on a business basis? the social security funds are in deficit because the state draws resources from social security funds to finance the money markets and gives gifts to employers through reductions in employer contributions. the proposed measures are likely to make the financial situation of the insurance funds more difficult. when social security is privatised, what kind of insurance will the 20% of the european union's population below the poverty line and the 8.8% of the unemployed have, according to a recent eurostat study? so the workers have nothing to look forward to from the much-publicized health insurance card. instead, they face greater insecurity, poverty and increased payments for prevention, health protection and care. we are confident that their struggle will overturn these policies. we, as the communist party of greece, stand with them.

priority of a very high level of protection of human health. it is a fact that tissues and cells contribute to the restoration of health on a daily basis and it is therefore necessary to define a cells in europe is greater than the availability. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rules on the protection of animals are respected. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. at the same time, the donation of human tissues and cells must be based on the free will of the donor and not on remuneration. the human body, as has been repeatedly stressed, is inviolable and recyclable, and should not be turned into a source of profit. the compromise reached in the negotiations satisfies the above principles. the addition that donors may receive compensation strictly limited to the reimbursement of the costs and the procedure related to the donation does not infringe the principle of voluntariness and allows member states to define the conditions under which compensation may be granted. it is also positive that in this directive, as in blood, the necessary data are stored to ensure traceability at all stages for at least thirty years after clinical use. the full and thorough information of the donor by a trained person concerning the purpose, relevant points in the annex. i would like to say, mr president, that although the package of compromise amendments does not include any other important points which have been approved by the the directive we are discussing is very important, mr president, perhaps it is the five-year directive. because we are not just saying 'the polluter pays', and therefore the polluter can pollute, but that the polluter must pay the cost of repairing the damage he has caused. the directive can therefore respond to the great hopes of our citizens for public health and the environment and we must not weaken it, mr president and ladies and gentlemen. there were differences of opinion during the debate. it has been shown that compromise solutions can be found, such as compulsory insurance being gradual but not passing the cost of the damage on to the taxpayer and allowing the polluter to cover the damage through insurance; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's environmental policy is not distorted by the introduction of new technologies, and that the community's environmental policy is not distorted by the introduction of new technologies. but we have problems which we cannot, it seems, find compromising solutions to. is it possible to speak of agricultural and forestry practices which can somehow justify the use of chemical fertilizers, pesticides and herbicides, when we all know - from the statistics of the union itself - the damage they can cause to biodiversity, soil and water?
